items.body: 山下達郎のライブアルバム『JOY 2 / TATSURO YAMASHITA LIVE』が2026年10月14日（水）にリリースされることが決定した。 ここ数年、ファンの間で渇望され、山下達郎本人の口からも制作状況が都度語られてきたライブアルバム『JOY 2 / TATSURO YAMASHITA LIVE』が遂に完成した。山下達郎のライブ盤は1978年に発売された『IT’S A POPPIN’ TIME』、1989年に発売された『JOY』の2作品に続き、通算3作目。前作『JOY』からはなんと37年ぶり、まさにファン待望のリリースとなる。 2008年から2025年までの18年間で実施した13本の全国ツアー、600を超える公演から山下達郎本人がベストオブベストテイクを厳選した、3枚組全38トラックで構成される本作。ディスク1には“SPARKLE”“DONUT SONG”“僕らの夏の夢”“土曜日の恋人”“風の回廊（コリドー）”“さよなら夏の日”“THE THEME FROM BIG WAVE”などライブには欠かせない定番曲に加え、初期の名作である“CIRCUS TOWN”や近年のヒットナンバー“SYNC OF SUMMER”まで16トラックが収められる。 ディスク2には“WINDY LADY”や“PAPER DOLL”“BOMBER”を挟んだ“SILENT SCREAMER”のほか、“恋のブギ・ウギ・トレイン”など山下達郎のライブの真骨頂とも言える10トラックを収録。 ディスク3には“人力飛行機”“ミライのテーマ”などの比較的新しめのナンバーに加え、“蒼氓（そうぼう）”“ずっと一緒さ”などの染み入るナンバー、さらには“高気圧ガール”“アトムの子”“RIDE ON TIME”などのタツロークラシックから最新曲“MOVE ON”まで幅広い選曲で12トラックが収められる。 また、初回盤にのみ付属するディスク4には、既発シングルのボーナストラックだったライブ音源6トラックが新たなミックスを施して収録されるほか、ツアーではおなじみの“LET’S DANCE BABY”のメドレー箇所だけをエディットした2010年、2012年、2014年のバージョンの3トラックも用意。合計9トラックというファン垂涎のボーナスディスクとなっている。 ソロデビュー50周年という節目の年に遂に登場するライブアルバム『JOY 2』。発売を楽しみに待とう。

items.body:
INTERNATIONAL（海外）
NEWS
豪州７都市を巡回「Japan Jazz Nights」
「日豪友好協力基本条約」署名50周年記念
2026年8月11日
編集部

「日豪友好協力基本条約」署名50周年を記念し2026年10月にオーストラリア７都市（アデレード、キャンベラ、シドニー、ホバート、パース、ブリスベン、メルボルン）を巡るジャズ巡回公演「Japan Jazz Nights」が予定されている。

この公演には、国際的にも注目を集める４組のアーティスト（BIGYUKI、STEREO CHAMP、Tenors In Chaos、梅井美咲）が出演、公演では一部、現地のアーティストとのコラボレーションも予定されており、音楽を通じて両国の相互理解を深め、日豪間の文化交流のさらなる発展を目指しているという。国際交流基金の交流事業の一環として実施される

items.body: If a tree falls in the forest, does it make a sound? And what if an entire forest falls? Around Here, The Birds Plant The Trees, inspired by a “clear-felled wasteland” in Leitrim, Ireland, amplifies these questions. In the digital era, it prompts an additional question: “When the liner notes are integral to the release, will listeners intuit the point?” We hope so, in the same manner as those hearing classical works over the centuries have gleaned the intentions of the composers, from “The Goldfinch” to The Four Seasons. In her first work for ensemble, Natalia Beylis uses different instruments to evoke “the rustle of beetles in the hedgerow, the squeak of a leaning Sitka spruce, a lone curlew’s call,” and her overall concern is that listeners will hear the richness of a richness of a landscape and be moved to protect it. While this landscape is incredibly specific: a single field on 12 December 2025, beginning at 6 a.m. ~ it could be any environment threatened by large multinational corporations, who swoop in to offer short-term recompense for long-term loss. Looking out over the field, Beylis notes the activity of a single blackbird, and later, an entire flock. Adding to the pathos is the fact that even birds are now endangered (for details, we recommend Robert Macfarlane & Jackie Morris’ The Book of Birds). If the music of the actual birds is inadequate to promote empathy, might music take up the cause? The alternative is to say nothing and to play nothing. As one might expect, the 51-minute piece is filled with intricate description and high drama. The cello’s low notes launch the piece in a reverent tone, considering at a field that once was a forest. As the other members of the string quartet join in, the nuance starts to develop. What began as drone becomes a harmonic suite with a distinctly Irish lilt. Then the first taps of percussion, like small creatures rustling through the grass, foraging for breakfast. A period of abstraction follows, during which every resident of field and forest receives their own spotlight. The blackbird eats and mates and cross-pollinates. The squirrels rush to and fro; the fox chases the shrew. All the while, the breeze threads through the branches of the hawthorn, creating a rhythm of leaves. The atmosphere seems peaceful until the thrums of the 15th minute, a soupçon of danger as most of the animals and instruments go into hiding. The contrast between presence and absence is integral to the composition. One feels the recession of sound as one might feel the destruction of trees. What was once lush becomes a hush, like the quietude of midday. Then the drone re-develops, a symbol of hope and regrowth. A vast cymbal strike like a gong at 32:07 interrupts the process, leaving only the drums and the wind in its wake. Willie Stewart’s work in this segment is enthralling; it sounds like architecture being built. But as the strings re-enter, are they busy as bees or as bulldozers? The listener is left to decide. Beylis initially planned to “write something to equal the harsh cacophony of the harvesting machines as they shred the nests of fledgling buzzards; to evoke the rumbling shaking noise I’d hear in bed at night as they crashed the huge trees they’d cut to the ground,” but relented for the sake of the blackbird. The dissonance that follows the drums suggests that the idea was not totally discarded. This makes the closing segment all the sweeter: consonance rising out of dissonance, form from chaos. The forest may have been leveled, but around here, the birds plant the trees. This being said, the story is not meant to encourage as much as it is to unsettle. Robert Plant once sang, “if there’s a bustle in your hedgerow, don’t be alarmed now.” Beylis has a different message: be alarmed. Be very alarmed. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Pentagrams Of Discordia seem to vaporize sound itself, blending traces of past, present, and future until their downtempo worlds begin to intertwine. Beats become memories, melodies become distant signals, and atmosphere takes over as the guiding force. Cryptic chapters buried deep within a book of shadows   Out of nowhere, and perhaps because of our curiosity about all things Pentagrams Of Discordia, Whispers About Radiance slips into view through three long-form pieces of nostalgic, downtempo analog production that feel less like compositions and more like an escape through lost time. Melancholic yet forward-thinking, propelled by atmosphere but steered by broken, disheveled beats, meandering tone clusters, and fractured rhythms, this sampler may showcase only three compositions, but it feels more like several cryptic chapters buried deep within a book of shadows. Darkness and sadness blur around the edges, as though POD can seamlessly traverse time and space, moving between half-remembered places and dream worlds without ever fully settling in one. Each chapter carries remarkable depth; off-kilter synths intertwine with shattered percussion while uplifting reverse-looped melodies and degraded rhythms slowly dissolve, reappear, and drift away like faded memories or solitary wanderings down memory lane. Nothing remains entirely fixed; sounds and voices emerge from the ha​ze, briefly take shape, then recede, leaving behind the feeling of having remembered something that never quite happened. These semi-pastiche soundtracks, steeped in BOC-laden sonic syrup and kaleidoscopic drift, form another wonderful collection for those who find comfort in music that refuses to reveal everything at once. Voices, samples, pulsing old-school beats, melodies, and wandering analog sequences trace a peculiar musical trajectory, buried beneath darkness yet constantly peering toward the light. Aptly titled, the album seems to whisper a transmission of light and energy from somewhere just beyond our vision, a surface deliberately left indistinct, perhaps because it was never meant to be fully understood. Circling through patterns that gradually mutate rather than resolve :: The slow-motion emotion of opener “Slowing of Evolution” unfolds across 18 minutes, conjuring fantastical stages of eroded sound that gradually take root and nurture the soul. Its movement is patient, but never static, allowing ambient passages and rhythmic fragments to guide one another through a landscape that feels both ancient and strangely futuristic. “Refrain of Dusk” maintains that slow-churning momentum, rugged drums collapsing into melodic shifts and subtle transitions while atmosphere remains firmly at its core. There is a sense of forward motion here, though it arrives more like drifting than traveling. Like reliving childhood memories, a few minutes at a time—waking up from one only to slowly fade into another. Closing piece “Loops of Entropy” is perhaps the most structured of the three, built around heavier-duty breaks and a more pronounced sense of mood. Its title quite literally evokes “cyclic processes or recursive loops tied to disorder and uncertainty,” and the music follows suit, circling through patterns that gradually mutate rather than resolve. What begins as something comparatively grounded slowly fragments, dissolving back into ambient propulsion. By the closing chapter, POD seem to vaporize sound itself, blending traces of past, present, and future until their downtempo worlds begin to intertwine. Beats become memories, melodies become distant signals, and atmosphere takes over as the guiding force. Eventually, all that remains is the urge to return and listen again, following layer upon layer as they hypnotize, unsettle, and reflect back some of the finest soundscapes and sound-scrapes we’ve heard this year. Whispers About Radiance (Sampler) is a precursor to the forthcoming August 28, 2026 album. [Bandcamp]  The post Pentagrams Of Discordia :: Whispers About Radiance (Sampler) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Tricky turns the difficult stuff into sound rather than sermon, and the result is an album that feels less like an elegy than a deeply lived affirmation of being here. No, not a return to form. The form was never abandoned. Instead, a deeply resonant expression of a singular experience eventually known finally by all. Alpha to Omega. A sonic symbol for the game of life Different When It's Silent by Tricky // False Idols   Actual legend Tricky has been on my radar since Massive Attack’s Blue Lines days, from “Karmacoma” and his forever-faultless first album Maxinquaye. I bought the digipack singles “Ponderosa” and “Aftermath,” and fell deeply for Alex Reece’s remix of “Brand New Retro.” To have his thirty-years-later work, Different When It’s Silent, on my figurative desk to write a commentary on is a foundationally humbling notion. Let’s be clear: there are no airs and graces about this new set of emotionally resonant tracks, and as a result, expect no airs and graces from this attempt to put into words a profoundly touched and cosmically imbibed album as Tricky presents here. From the outset there is a cornerstone of authenticity that I’m not sure Tricky could avoid for all the money in the world. If heart-on-the-sleeve were a creative pulse—and it often is, and if I had my way always would be—then this album, and its purveyor, Tricky, are the embodiment of that same intention. Even if a person were not an artist and were merely a voyeur of any form of art, authenticity would be the facet they would recognize without necessarily knowing they were in its presence. Authenticity is the key to reaching into the place within an audience member that an artist desires to touch: the artist channels the piece they are working ​on by paying attention to the creative pulse as it moves through them. That symmetry, that resonance, is beyond the control of artist and audience. But when it is channeled to the degree to which it is here, the creative piece simply appears. This notion should not undermine the capacity to pay attention to the creative whorl as it passes through the creator of the work. With the intent of a fractured but reassembled vase for life, Tricky neatly assembles, in simple terms, a group of local and distant cohorts, and a rudimentary application of post-rock, trip-hop beats, rhymes and loves for life—either here or there—forming perhaps the most cohesive fractured, broken and complete incompleteness: a sonic symbol for the game of life.   A neat hybridization of acoustic and sampled work :: Vocal duties are shared between Mitch Saunders’ beautiful falsetto, Run Red Rambo’s tight bars, Radana’s gravitas, False Idol’s own Marta Zlakowska, and Tricky himself. The musical palette is a neat hybridization of acoustic and sampled work. Throbbing bass pulses across tribal tom rhythms; atmospheres and tones are melancholic, adding to that same emotional heft. Moods move between optimism and broken-heartedness: crying to be seen and pleading to be heard wrestle alongside hope for the future and the feeling of being alive after retreating for an undisclosed time. After all, no one is immune to life, right? In places such as “Be Still in the Pain,” there is self-aware anger against loss and presence. On the frankly astounding “Piano,” choral laments parry against Mitch’s tender lament. “Marinade”—string quartet and Tricky’s vocal musing—paints a wonderful canvas for realness personified. And Marta’s appearance on closing track “Out of Place” is frankly stunning. In the end, it’s an open heart that opens the heart. It’s delightfully real. And Tricky’s paean to his daughter carries a weight that makes the whole record feel suddenly more human, more fragile. There is something profoundly moving in hearing someone arrive at that place where love, absence and mortality occupy the same space—where the knowledge that nothing and no one can be held onto forever becomes not an abstraction, but something lived and felt. Yet the album doesn’t dwell there. Instead, that awareness seems to feed back into the music itself: the warmth of the acoustic elements, the bruised electronics, the fractured rhythms, the choral textures and those beautifully human voices all become part of the same emotional vocabulary. Mortality is present, certainly, but so is life in all its messy, sensual, rhythmic immediacy. Tricky turns the difficult stuff into sound rather than sermon, and the result is an album that feels less like an elegy than a deeply lived affirmation of being here. No, not a return to form. The form was never abandoned. Instead, a deeply resonant expression of a singular experience eventually known finally by all. Alpha to Omega. Different When It’s Silent is available on False Idols. [Bandcamp] Different When It's Silent by Tricky // False Idols  The post Tricky :: Different When It’s Silent (False Idols) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Fruupp, for years lived under the shadows of giants, as an opening act for bands like Genesis orKing Crimson, working hard to get recognition, the quintet was prolific in every sense of the word,and despite never getting any commercial success, some of their influence can be felt on genres suchas math rock or symphonic prog.Before the actual review starts, I'd like to take a moment to do something I am not acostumed to inthis site, I'd like to give the band some extra points for their wonderful sleeve art, which is aninteresting mix of medieval, impressionist and dadaist styles...unlike many eclectic covers whichare absurd for the sake for absurdity itself, this cover is absurd but also hides intention andartistic quality, anyone dedicated enough to aesthetics will get what I mean. It's a beautifulsleeve indeed.Starting off with that which is the absolute strength of this record : It's creativity and uniqueapproach. Northern Ireland had been a colony under British imperial rule for quite a while at thatpoint, so it's natural that aspects of cultural syncretism are to be felt across the 39 minutes ofmusic this album has, yet, it keeps most of the Irish musical identity intact, this is an act ofcultural resistance, but mixed with a proper dose of syncretism, it feels innovative, if they hadgone a little more British, then it would have hit the uncanny valley, yet this is not the case. Iwas quite surprised to learn that this band is not Iberian either, since strangely enough some ofthe modes, scales and rhythmic patterns are borrowed from Iberian music, this adds to a refreshingMediterranean sound mixed with strong Celtic influence, it's white funny how well these two stylesfit together in the record, since it *shouldn't* be that way as their almost opposite philosophiesin the way they approach this art. I also noticed some faint Arabic influences, but they are smalland barely noticeable, it's on tracks such as "Graveyard Epistle" where it can truly be felt...butit might as well just be the Iberian influence I mentioned before, since iberia is stronglyinfluenced by the Arab world due go the 700 years it spent under Arabic rule.The quality of the compositions is rich and diverse, despite being relatively short (between the 4and 8 minutes mark), they have several small movements, leitmotifs and variations, it's rhythmicallydense and that's it's clearest identity factor, across the record, the intricate and delicatepercussions, bass lines and guitars are condensed in a dance and struggle against each other,pushing to their limits and then coming together in complex polyrhythms, metrics and lines thatsyncopate and then go into chaos, over and over, it's hypnotic! The track "Song for a thought" is agreat example of this, it also incorporates classic Rock and roll elements. Then comes theambientation, oboes, string ensembles, delayed and reversed guitars and some clicking cymbals createan ambience of immersion and psychedelia which is ethereal in nature, it induces a high state ofconcentration and doesn't contradict the complex rhythms, if anything it complements them.If I had to describe the sound of this record in a single sentence it'd be : Baroque andmulticultural, vanguardist yet hypnotic...feels fresh even in 2026, which is 50+ years since it'srelease.The musicianship is great, and there's a natural chemistry between them all that holds thecompositions together like a glue, they are technically prominent (although not gifted) and have agreat sense of melody and rhythm, their teamwork is astonishing, specially the lead singers voicewhich is similar to Lake from ELP and Shulman from gentle giant. The production is okay, it doesfeel rough and noisy at times but putting this into context (underground act mainly known by collegestudents in Britain) it's understandable, it's something you can distract from if you will, andprobably will do so anyways because of how hypnotic this all is.Fans of gentle giant will love this since it feels a lot like "Acquiring the taste" (specially theslower, violin driven parts), the similarities are astounding, the band had not yet reached theirfull identity yet, but it's enjoyable anyways.A solid 5/5!

items.album: Event Review: WOMAD 2026 @ Neston Park (Corsham, Wiltshire; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026)
items.excerpt: There is a certain tenor a WOMAD stalwart comes to expect: a practiced routine, a beaten track past well-known landmarks, a familiarity akin to coming home. Sometimes it’s good to mix it up a bit. items.body: There is a certain tenor a WOMAD stalwart comes to expect: a practiced routine, a beaten track past well-known landmarks, a familiarity akin to coming home. Sometimes it’s good to mix it up a bit. This July marked the festival’s first edition in a new location just up the road from Charlton Park, its much-loved site for 17 happy years before taking a break in 2025. Organisers have been quick to reassure returnees that they’ll find the new spot welcoming and Neston Park, just half an hour away in Corsham, does indeed have a home-from-home feel, the flutter of those familiar flags helping crowds settle quickly into the weekend. Some old favourites are missing: the d&b Soundscape stage with its state-of-the-art surround-sound experience; late night party venue Molly’s Bar; the Ecotricity stage, a cosy woodland spot for daytime respite or atmospheric after-dark shows; the magical Hidden Forest lit up by Luke Jerram’s Moon; the World of Science (a niche interest perhaps but a favourite, inevitably, of some). WOMAD kicks off at its brand new site at Neston Park, marking a new chapter for the independent World of Music and Dance Festival – Photo © garryjonesphotography So it is left to the music to carry the show and here the new compactness comes into its own, the smaller tents packed with hidden gems and standout performances of the festival which has not skimped on its musical programme at least. The main stages offer up a mixed bag of hits and misses, occasionally mired by murky sound and drab set design. On the World Stage the effervescent Derya Yıldırım, her voice in turns aching, wistful and full of soul, is supported by the psychedelic squelchy synth and phenomenally groovy rhythm section of her Grup Şimşek. It is sun-drenched and beautiful, augmented by her call for freedom, cultural strength and acceptance for those dwelling in the diaspora. Bristol’s Ishmael Ensemble seem warm in their black outfits, camouflaged against a black stage and backdrop and playing directly into the sun’s heat. Perhaps this explains the low energy feel of both band and scattered crowd. Their jazz-inspired saxophone-and-synth jams with Rituals ‘Orchestra’ (comprising two violins, a harp and a cello) is lacking oomph. A smaller stage may well have inspired bigger vibes. Reggae legend Barrington Levy takes to the World Stage at WOMAD festival – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography Reggae icon Barrington Levy is welcomed by a vast, multi-generational crowd and while there are a few unconvincing moments from a seemingly under-rehearsed band (as well as a smattering of problematic lyrical content sometimes associated with reggae that predates the 80s), his voice is as smooth and powerful as ever, his scatting as wild and his strut as convincing, especially on 2025’s ‘A Fi Yuh’. Eventually, the crowd is galvanised into repeatedly requesting “run the track” while Levy teases ‘Black Roses’ and ‘Here I Come’ until well beyond his stage time, berating the MC for clock-watching and singing on until his mic is turned off. The night’s headliner Greentea Peng calls “I love you Barry” and apes his vocal riffing throughout her glorious 90-minute show. An all-round class act, her band provide tasteful support for her elegant, honey-smothered r’n’b, with a high calibre all-female brass section ramping up the energy and spectacle. Greentea Peng headlining WOMAD Festival – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography On Saturday, Mixanteña de Santa Cecilia from Mexico City treat a packed Big Top to a classic slice of WOMAD with a high energy fusion of costumed dancers, ritualistic set pieces, eight-piece brass section and percussion. Their mix of cumbia, bossa nova and boleros is full of life, while joyful dancers in long-haired ram-horned headdress and twirling petticoats cause a stir when their bull puppet is sent in to dance with the crowd. It is experiences like these that keep people returning year on year. Similarly, Bénin International Musical provide the perfect sunny soundtrack to a hot afternoon, the disco pop harmonies of Say She She floating across the field give the sense that all is right with this world of music and dance, and Nakibembe Xylophone Troupe are hotly tipped as this year’s mustn’t-miss sensation. Ugandan Nakimbembe Xylophone Troupe bring their 3 metres long embaire to WOMAD, the largest instrument to grace the festivals stages, played by 6 members – Photo © garryjonesphotography But it is the Sunflower stage, a stretch tent conveniently located to break up the just-too-arduous walk between the two main stages, that provides the weekend’s first nugget of pure gold. Tamer Nafar, one third of Palestinian hip hop trio DAM, is flanked for this solo appearance by a beat maker and exquisite Arabic-influenced electric violinist. Nafar is a warm presence with powerful words, throwing out politically charged statements and personal anecdotes with equal emotive power. His latest record, In the Name of the Father, the Imam and John Lennon, references the two CDs his dad would play when driving him to underground rap clubs: the Beatles and the Quran. “But we don’t have to imagine there’s no country”, a defiant teenage Nafar said back then, but he’s retained his love of the seminal Liverpudlians. LYR (Land Yacht Regatta, inexplicably) draw big numbers to that same tent, primarily to catch celebrity poet Simon Armitage in his new musical guise, his downbeat musings backed by pulsing bass and suitably moody, introspective soundscapes. His dry Yorkshire humour goes down well between songs and the crowd responds enthusiastically to the band’s paean to libraries, ‘The Enlightenment’, in particular. Tamer Nafar, a vanguard of Arabic Hip-Hop, the Palestinian rapper living in Israel performs a selection of tracks discussing Middle East politics & life at WOMAD – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography The even smaller Village Stage, tucked away in a corner next to second mainstage the Big Top, boasts some of the best acts of the weekend. For only their second live show, Romanian seven-piece Lăutăresele Șaraimanic pull out all the stops with high glamour and captivating dancing drawing on the Turkish and Roma heritage of their homeland. Accordionist Mituș Răducanu, the oldest group member, steals the show with his delighted toothy grins. Later in the day, Belarusian Yegor Zabelov keeps the audience riveted with his expansive world-building, pushing the accordion to new creative limits with drones, sound walls and percussion sounds. And sparky Portuguese solo artist Ana Lua Caiano grabs attention with her melodramatic delivery, then holds it with impressive looping of synth, percussion and voice into multilayered epics of fiery emotion. A stunned audience of all ages watch each song construction with awe, then explode in applause as Caiano expresses her deep delight and gratitude. Lautaresele Saraimanic at Village Stage performing at WOMAD Festival – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography The sentiment was one that emanated across the site as another WOMAD was put to bed. Dynamic, welcoming, vibrating with fighting spirit and above all full of joy and connection, the 2026 edition served as a reminder of the role the festival plays in building community and educating through creativity. Pre-sale tickets for 2027 have already sold out. Perhaps this year’s success will instil organisers with the confidence to bring back some of the site’s sorely missed old favourites; or, more in keeping with the culture of the event, to surprise us with something wholly new and unexpected.   Pre-sale tickets for 2027 have already sold out, but you can keep in the loop for the next batch over at womad.co.uk     Photos © garryjonesphotography The post Event Review: WOMAD 2026 @ Neston Park (Corsham, Wiltshire; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: “Natural” moves at walking pace, a lovers rock groove kept soft under Clarence Bekker‘s blues-trained voice as it eases across the rocksteady sway. The new single from his Barcelona band is a plain love song from a singer with a long, loud history behind him. Bekker carries an unusual CV for a reggae singer: a UK chart entry in the 1990s as CB Milton, seven world tours, and a spell fronting the street-recorded Playing For Change project. Born in Suriname and raised in the Netherlands from the age of six, he cut his teeth in the Dutch group Swinging Soul Machine before that dance-pop run, then settled in Barcelona and, in 2016, built a band around local players. That band is a five-piece of Barcelona regulars: guitarist Francisco Guisado, known as Rubio, keyboardist Arecio Smith, bassist Charlie Cuevas and drummer Carlos López behind Bekker’s vocals. They hold a weekly Thursday residency at the jazz club Jamboree and have carried the same lineup as far as Australia and Brazil. The song came together between Barcelona and the road, Bekker recording while Irish lyricist Michael Leahy sent words over from wherever he was travelling, a habit going back to their fax-machine days writing CB Milton hits together in the 90s. Everyone in the band had a hand in it, and it holds to the idea in its title: an unhurried love song, played the easy way. It is the first single from an album due later this year. Listen to “Natural” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Clarence Bekker Band – Natural appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.album: Against The Grain: Collective listening events
items.excerpt: Collective listening events respond to a cultural need, but are at risk of co-option by wellness and lifestyle marketeers, argues Derek Walmsley in The Wire 511 “You’re in the right place!” smiles the man in the smart shirt and trousers at the velvet rope line. items.body: Collective listening events respond to a cultural need, but are at risk of co-option by wellness and lifestyle marketeers, argues Derek Walmsley in The Wire 511 “You’re in the right place!” smiles the man in the smart shirt and trousers at the velvet rope line. Inside a modest door on a touristy street in London’s Soho is a cocktail bar, work space, podcast studio, plus a private cinema which doubles as Polygon Portal, a high spec surround sound listening venue. The occasion is John Coltrane’s centenary, and his Impulse! albums A Love Supreme and John Coltrane And Johnny Hartman are being played for an audience of around 50 people lounging on soft seats and sofas with blindfolds to block out distractions. A ticket costs £25. These kinds of immersive listening experiences are finding an audience. At Polygon Portal, many of their events – which include classic album sessions, curated playlists accompanied by a short history essay, and “wellbeing” events with some kind of meditation or ritual – are sold out. The vibe in the bar beforehand falls somewhere between the taut anticipation of a classy date and the insider chit-chat behind the counter at a record shop. Even if you’ve heard A Love Supreme dozens of times, you pick up something new here. The Polygon set-up takes the original recording and diffuses it across an array of speakers, keeping the stereo separation but allocating frequencies to various cones, tweeters and subwoofers. This particular event does not use surround sound, which might distribute the four instruments of Coltrane’s classic quartet to discrete audio sources around the venue. But the distinction between the players is still impressive, seeming to occupy different areas of the room. The rhythm section of Elvin Jones and Jimmy Garrison in particular comes alive, the vibrations in the air carrying a churning turbulence absent on hi-fi or headphones. Pitchblack Playback is another listening gathering, with events in cities across several continents. A London event includes a free Joni Mitchell eye mask to help you concentrate on Blue (55th anniversary version) and Court And Spark, and there’s even a recorded message from Joni beforehand. There are rules to help everyone get along: no looking at phones, no singing, no latecomers. You commit to listening to each album in its entirety, which strengthens the sense of its structure and logic. Afterwards, my smartphone tells me my heartbeat dropped into a state of deep relaxation over the course of the session. Listening to albums together in public is nothing new. Recorded Music Societies blossomed in the postwar period in the UK, where church halls or libraries hosted gatherings for people to hear records without needing to own costly equipment, with the addition perhaps of an informative talk. London audiophile venue Spiritland opened a decade ago, and in the years since, other listening bars in the city such as Brilliant Corners, Jazu, One Eighty One and the Listening Room at 180 Studios have all offered music heads a place to bond over records. Collective listening experiences address a desire that many feel for a sense of community – seen elsewhere in the renewed interest in crafting, workshops and real life social networks – and for discovering culture outside the circles of apps and algorithms. This demand side now meets a supply side where cinemas and other high street spaces are underused in the post-pandemic era, and London residents often have limited space in their own homes. While it might seem odd to spend a chunk of money to hear music you might easily find online, it scratches a particular itch for some. Immersive listening events often carry a sense of exclusivity. Some sell themselves as part of a digital detox – there are events with guided meditation, yoga, or singing bowls – and while the marketing patter might allude to community and connection, presenting themselves as a sanctuary from the world outside can be read as a kind of snobbery. The idea of getting away from the online world easily blurs into a humblebrag about an enviable alternative lifestyle. The Japanese idea of the jazz kissa – a cafe with a library-like atmosphere in which to appreciate jazz records in particular – gives an extra vibe of distinction to some listening venues. At a time when these venues sometimes struggle for relevance in Japan in the era of the smartphone, their Western iterations have become suddenly chic and fetishised, providing an aspirational oasis of Eastern calm with ticket prices to match. This kind of branding plays out on Instagram and other social media channels, despite the promise that listening venues constitute a break from online life. Polygon Portal have ambitious ideas. They plan to parlay the attraction of spatial audio into nightclub, restaurant and even gym destinations. These would no doubt all be beautiful experiences, but the more chic the marketing pitch gets, the more alienating some may find it. At present, listening events often look backwards. Many of the albums featured in immersive listening sessions crop up as they hit an anniversary, or emerge in a glossy new reissue. While that helps to fill venues with committed fans, it also creates a somewhat predictable merry-go-round of familiar classics. As with any artistic canon, unless it’s refreshed, stretched and tested, it feels destined to become stale. For immersive sound experiences to fulfil their creative potential, they need to be open and accessible, firstly to different audiences, and also to relationships with other bodies. A varied approach to curation would ensure that legacy rock reissues don’t dominate the music that’s presented. And reaching out to other organisations might make them less exclusive, more connected to culture’s grassroots, and give them a broader social mission. There’s a future in which DIY organisations, festivals, collectives, multi-disciplinary bodies and other cultural incubators use collective listening to forge stronger connections between audiences and music. If listeners are revisiting King Crimson or Joni Mitchell, why not the music of Terry Riley, Pharoah Sanders, Julius Eastman, Maryanne Amacher, Pauline Oliveros, Alvin Lucier, or any number of avant garde or experimental touchstones? By exploring music found off the beaten track, these kinds of events could serve to change and refresh canons, and not just replicate them. This essay appears in The Wire 511. Wire subscribers can also read it in our online magazine library.

items.body: Slovenian industrial group Laibach will give “Die Kanone”, its collaboration with Bijelo Dugme, a first physical release on October 30, 2026, via Matrix Music Arhiv (MMA), distributed through Audioglobe. The release comes on two vinyl editions and a digipak CD, and follows the digital-only single Laibach issued via Mute in July 2025. “Die Kanone” reworks “Top” (“The Cannon”), the first single Bijelo Dugme released in 1974, recast by Laibach in German for a collaboration initiated by Bijelo Dugme founder and songwriter Goran Bregović to mark that band’s 50th anniversary. The October 30 release adds the track’s Slovenian-language version, “S topom te bom ciljal moja mala” (“I’ll Aim My Cannon at You, My Little One”), together with previously unreleased remixes by German industrial and EBM act Die Krupps, UK producer the Lincolnshire Poacher, and Slovenian-Croatian electronic duo Black Dot. Both the German and Slovenian versions are being made available on a physical format for the first time. The vinyl LP is issued in a limited green edition and a standard black edition, both carrying the same six tracks: “Die Kanone”, “S topom te bom ciljal moja mala”, the Die Krupps remix, the Lincolnshire Poacher mix, the Black Dot version, and a live recording of “Die Kanone” performed with the RTV Slovenia Symphony Orchestra at the Ljubljana Opera. The CD, released as a digipak, carries all six tracks plus two exclusive bonus cuts not available on vinyl: a live version of “S topom te bom ciljal moja mala” recorded at the same Ljubljana Opera performance, and a karaoke version of “Die Kanone”. ‘Die Kanone’ tracklist across formats Vinyl LP (green and black editions): A1 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – 3:03 A2 “S topom te bom ciljal moja mala (I’ll Aim My Cannon at You, My Little One)” – 3:01 A3 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – Die Krupps remix – 3:41 B1 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – the Lincolnshire Poacher mix – 5:18 B2 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – Black Dot version – 4:34 B3 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – live at the Opera with RTV Slovenia Symphony Orchestra – 3:05 Digipak CD: 01 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – 3:03 02 “S topom te bom ciljal moja mala (I’ll Aim My Cannon at You, My Little One)” – 3:01 03 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – Die Krupps remix – 3:41 04 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – the Lincolnshire Poacher mix – 5:18 05 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – Black Dot version – 4:34 06 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – live at the Opera with RTV Slovenia Symphony Orchestra – 3:05 07 “S topom te bom ciljal moja mala (I’ll Aim My Cannon at You, My Little One)” – live at the Opera – 2:51 08 “Die Kanone (The Cannon)” – karaoke version – 2:52 About Laibach Laibach was formed in 1980 in Trbovlje, Slovenia, then part of Yugoslavia, by Dejan Knez, Milan Fras, Ervin Markošek and Ivan Novak. The group positioned itself from the outset as a multimedia collective, pairing martial industrial sound with provocative imagery, performance art and sociopolitical critique, and later became the musical wing of the Neue Slowenische Kunst art collective. After early cassette releases, Laibach’s debut album appeared on ŠKUC ROPOT in 1985. International attention followed a signing to Mute Records, which released “Opus Dei” in 1987, featuring reworkings of Queen’s “One Vision” and the Austrian national anthem “Geburt einer Nation”. Laibach has maintained a steady release pace since, with albums including “NATO” (1994), “Volk” (2006) and “Spectre” (2014), and has worked with symphonic ensembles and experimental artists on projects such as “Also sprach Zarathustra” and, more recently, “Alamut” with A/Political. In 2015, Laibach became the first Western band to perform in North Korea. The group’s 2026 studio album “Musick” was released via Mute earlier this year, following a 2026 European tour. The current lineup includes Milan Fras, Ivan Novak, Luka Jamnik and Rok Lopatič. Laibach initiated its collaboration with Bijelo Dugme – the Sarajevo rock band founded by Goran Bregović in 1974 whose original 1974 single “Top” is reworked on “Die Kanone” – at Bregović’s request, to mark Bijelo Dugme’s 50th anniversary. The two acts first released “Die Kanone” digitally via Mute and Classic Records in July 2025. The October 30, 2026 release on Matrix Music Arhiv brings the collaboration to vinyl and CD for the first time, adding the Slovenian-language version and three new remixes alongside a live recording made with the RTV Slovenia Symphony Orchestra at the Ljubljana Opera.

items.body: Swiss avant-garde project KiKu will release its new album Suzhou / It’s All The Rage on Everest Records on September 25, 2026, on LP and CD. The album features Blixa Bargeld, founder and vocalist of Einstürzende Neubauten, and Berlin-based rapper and vocalist Black Cracker. “Suzhou / It’s All The Rage” is built as a diptych: two distinct halves held together by a shared musical architecture of trumpet, drums, sampler and electronics. The digital release and CD present the work as a continuous eight-track album. On vinyl, the dual structure becomes physical, with Side A carrying “Suzhou” featuring Bargeld and Side B carrying “It’s All The Rage” featuring Black Cracker. On “Suzhou”, Bargeld’s vocals move between speech, song, whisper and abstract vocal gesture across four tracks shaped by space, tension and control. On “It’s All The Rage”, Black Cracker’s vocals take a more percussive, volatile and immediate approach across the remaining four tracks. The tracklist runs: Suzhou – KiKu feat. Blixa Bargeld – Orlando’s Victory – 4:06 – The Number of the Millibeast – 4:48 – Suzhou (XX XY YX YY) – 4:16 – Nonsense Rock’n’Roll – 4:58 It’s All The Rage – KiKu feat. Black Cracker – Bull Whip – 3:36 – Leaping Bull (Chicago) – 5:05 – The Running of the Bulls – 3:50 – Sleeping Bull (Woke) – 4:32 Vocals and lyrics on tracks 1-4 are by Blixa Bargeld. Vocals and lyrics on tracks 5-8 are by Black Cracker. David Doyon plays guitar on tracks 2-4, and Cyril Regamey plays drums and sampler throughout. Bargeld’s vocals were recorded by Boris Wilsdorf at andereBaustelle Tonstudio, Berlin. Black Cracker recorded his own vocals, which were edited and mixed by Jane Arnison in Berlin. Drums were recorded by Antoine Estoppey at Blend Studio, Lutry, and trumpet and computer parts by Yannick Barman at Printemps Digital Studio, Monthey. The album was mixed by Barman and mastered by Estoppey at Blend Studio. Artwork and graphic design are by Cédric Raccio at La Fabrik, Monthey, and the photo of Bargeld is by Thomas Rabsch. About KiKu KiKu was founded in 2003 in Sion, Switzerland, by trumpeter and composer Yannick Barman and drummer and percussionist Cyril Regamey. The pair started as an acoustic improvisation duo, and their sound turned toward electronic music during a run of concerts at the Théâtre de l’Oriental in Vevey in February 2003. Since then, KiKu has operated as an open, modular formation that changes line-up and musical language with each project, working across contemporary jazz, electronic music, rock, improvised music and experimental sound art. The group has toured internationally, performing at jazz clubs and festivals across Europe and Asia as well as in Australia, and has previously collaborated with Blixa Bargeld and Black Cracker on the albums “Marcher sur la tête” (2015) and “Eng, Düster und Bang” (2017), both on Everest Records. Bargeld founded Einstürzende Neubauten in Berlin in 1980 and was also a member of Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds from 1983 to 2003. Black Cracker, born Ellison Glenn in Anniston, Alabama, is a rapper, producer and vocalist based in Berlin who also performs with the Swiss jazz trio Grand Pianoramax. “Suzhou / It’s All The Rage” extends KiKu’s collaboration with both vocalists into a new full-length release on Everest Records.

items.body: Stephan Groth, founder and vocalist of Apoptygma Berzerk, turns 55 on August 10, 2026. The Norwegian EBM and synthpop act, which Groth has led since 1989, marks the birthday alongside “Kathy’s Song XXV,” a 25th-anniversary reissue campaign built around one of the band’s best-known tracks, “Kathy’s Song (Come Lie Next to Me).” Groth was born on August 10, 1971, in Odense, Denmark, and relocated with his family to Sarpsborg, Norway, in 1986. He founded Apoptygma Berzerk in 1989 together with Jon Erik Martinsen, taking the band’s name from a word picked at random out of a dictionary, derived from the Ancient Greek for “piece of a tunic.” Martinsen left the group early on, and Groth has remained its sole constant member and main songwriter since. The band’s first two albums, “Soli Deo Gloria” (1993) and “7” (1996), established a darker EBM and electropop sound. “Welcome to Earth” (2000) moved toward a lighter, more experimental style and included “Kathy’s Song (Come Lie Next to Me),” built around a vocoded chorus voiced by Kathy Macintosh. The single followed on December 11, 2000, with a remix from Ferry Corsten that became a trance-scene favorite and helped push the song beyond the EBM and futurepop audience. “Harmonizer” (2002) leaned further into synthpop, “You and Me Against the World” (2005) took the band toward an indie rock-oriented sound, “Rocket Science” followed in 2009, and “Exit Popularity Contest” (2016) returned to the band’s earlier electronic roots. Beyond Apoptygma Berzerk, Groth has recorded as H2O with Geir Bratland in the mid-1990s and is a member of Fairlight Children, a lighter, pop-oriented electronic project that issued a limited vinyl edition of its “808Bit” album in February 2025. 2026 has brought “Kathy’s Song (Come Lie Next to Me)” back into focus. The 25th-anniversary “Kathy’s Song XXV” edition arrived digitally in December 2025, first on Bandcamp and then across other platforms, with new remixes by Ferry Corsten – who reworked his original 2000 remix – alongside Per Martinsen (Mental Overdrive) and Alyxx Digre (Zone Tripper). Groth has said the track is “probably the most important song I have ever written,” and described the vocoded chorus, recorded with Fredrik Darum and Vegard Blomberg, as something that “had never been done before” at the time. A physical follow-up arrived via emmobiz with a limited vinyl reissue, released on July 10, 2026. Stephan Groth marks 55th birthday as Apoptygma Berzerk celebrates ‘Kathy’s Song’ anniversary The overlap of Groth’s 55th birthday with the ongoing “Kathy’s Song” anniversary campaign places two Apoptygma Berzerk milestones in the same year. Side-Line previously covered the band’s 25th anniversary of “Soli Deo Gloria” with the “SDGXXV” reissue project in 2018, a similar reworking of an early album that Groth has cited as a direct model for how the “Kathy’s Song XXV” campaign was organized. About Apoptygma Berzerk Apoptygma Berzerk was founded in Norway in 1989 by Stephan Groth and Jon Erik Martinsen. Martinsen departed soon after, leaving Groth as the band’s vocalist, programmer, guitarist and sole constant member. The band’s debut album, “Soli Deo Gloria,” was released in 1993 and established a dark EBM and electropop sound, followed by “7” in 1996. Geir Bratland joined on keyboards in 1995, having already worked with Groth on the ambient techno side project H2O in the mid-1990s. “Welcome to Earth” arrived in 2000, softening the band’s earlier darker themes and including “Kathy’s Song (Come Lie Next to Me),” with vocals by Kathy Macintosh and a single release that December featuring a Ferry Corsten remix. “Harmonizer” followed in 2002 in a more synthpop-oriented direction, and “You and Me Against the World” (2005) marked a more mainstream, indie rock-influenced turn for the band, a departure the group revisited with expanded reissues in 2021. “Rocket Science” was released in 2009, and “Exit Popularity Contest” (2016) returned to the band’s earlier electronic and EBM-rooted sound. Alongside Apoptygma Berzerk, Groth has recorded as H2O with Bratland and continues as a member of Fairlight Children, a lighter, pop-oriented electronic project. The band marked the 25th anniversary of “Soli Deo Gloria” with the “SDGXXV” reimagining released in 2018 and 2019, and has since applied the same approach to “Kathy’s Song,” releasing the “Kathy’s Song XXV” remix EP in December 2025 and a limited vinyl edition in July 2026. Stephan Groth turns 55 on August 10, 2026, with more than 35 years of Apoptygma Berzerk behind him and, by his own account, new material still in progress.

items.album: Ayria announces new album ’13 Stitches’ on Artoffact Records

The 13-track digital and CD release ships on Compact Disc in a jewel box with an 8-page booklet of photography and in a limited deluxe CD box with bonus postcards and stickers; the vinyl LP, pressed on solid pink, carries an 11-track cut, “11 Stitches,” made to fit the format, with the full 13-track album included
items.body: Ayria, the Toronto electro-pop, EBM and futurepop project of Jennifer Parkin, will release the album “13 Stitches” on October 2, 2026 through Artoffact Records. The 13-track digital and CD release ships on Compact Disc in a jewel box with an 8-page booklet of photography and in a limited deluxe CD box with bonus postcards and stickers; the vinyl LP, pressed on solid pink, carries an 11-track cut, “11 Stitches,” made to fit the format, with the full 13-track album included as a digital download. Ayria bring an EBM and futurepop sound that mixes stomping electronic rhythms with pop hooks and personal, confrontational lyrics, and Parkin describes “13 Stitches” as a record of personal rebirth. The album was produced and mastered by Sebastian R. Komor at Xenomorph Production Studio, with additional contributions from Komor and Joe Byer of v01d. Its tracklist runs “Feeding Your Monsters,” “Turn of the Tide,” “Not My First Time,” “Long Gone,” “Vicious World,” “Manic,” “Antihero,” “Trickle Truth,” “Don’t Ever Touch Me Again,” “Overturn,” “We’re Not Relevant,” “Mr. Morals” and “Turn Into Gold.” The vinyl edition omits “We’re Not Relevant” and “Turn Into Gold” to fit the format. 13 Stitches by Ayria Ayria’s ‘Vicious World’ single ahead of ’13 Stitches’ Ayria shared “Vicious World” as the lead single from “13 Stitches,” with an official video pairing the track’s EBM stomp and repetition with dark, visceral visuals. About Ayria Ayria is the project of Toronto musician Jennifer Parkin, formed in 2003. Her debut album, “Debris,” followed later that year, with “My Revenge on the World” and “Flicker” in 2005, “Hearts for Bullets” on Alfa Matrix in 2008, “Plastic Makes Perfect” in 2013 and “Paper Dolls” in 2016, the last of which Side-Line covered as it was announced on CD, 2CD and fuchsia vinyl after the single “Feed Her to the Wolves.” Parkin discussed her approach to songwriting and production in a 2016 interview with Side-Line, and toured North America and the UK alongside Inertia that same year. Ayria signed to Artoffact Records in 2020 and most recently released the “Vicious World” EP, which Side-Line reviewed, ahead of “13 Stitches,” due October 2, 2026.

items.body: Soft Vein, the California-based electronic project of Justin Chamberlain, will release his third studio album, “All We’ve Known of Heaven,” on September 4, 2026 through Artoffact Records. The album arrives on a limited dark blue vinyl LP and on CD in a jewel box with booklet, alongside digital and streaming formats. Soft Vein bring a sound that mixes synthpop and sophisti-pop, with lush synthesizers, sparkling guitars and melodic vocals set against themes of nostalgia, romance, homesickness, personal growth and change. “All We’ve Known of Heaven” is co-produced by Soft Vein and Andrea Mantione of Nuovo Testamento, mixed by Chamberlain himself, and mastered by Jason Corbett of ACTORS at Jacknife Sound in Vancouver. Saxophonist Rachel Mazer guests on two tracks. The eight-track album runs “Another Summer,” “Chekhov,” “Learning to Talk,” “Proof of Life,” “White Towers (White Shores),” “Forgetting You,” “Living in Liminal Spaces” and the title track, “All We’ve Known of Heaven.” All We’ve Known of Heaven by Soft Vein Soft Vein’s title-track video for ‘All We’ve Known of Heaven’ Chamberlain shared an official video for “All We’ve Known of Heaven,” directed by Sydney Mills with cinematography by Cameron Dunbar. About Soft Vein Soft Vein is the solo electronic project of Los Angeles-based songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Justin Chamberlain. The project broke into the Los Angeles darkwave scene with a pair of early singles before signing to Artoffact Records and releasing its debut album, “Pressed in Glass,” in October 2023. Chamberlain followed with the second album, “Through Blinds,” in January 2025 and the EP “From Another Room” in June 2025, alongside the singles “Chekhov” and “All We’ve Known of Heaven” earlier in 2026. “All We’ve Known of Heaven,” due September 4, 2026, marks Soft Vein’s third full-length and was recorded during winter 2025/2026 at Seahorse Sound in Los Angeles and Jacknife Sound in Vancouver.

items.body: Schrödinger, the post-punk duo from Mexico City, released their second studio album, “International Decay,” digitally on July 26, 2026 through Swiss Dark Nights. The label follows with physical editions on September 4, 2026: a regular black vinyl LP, a limited white vinyl LP with red splatters capped at 250 copies, and a CD in digipak with a booklet containing lyrics and additional artwork. Schrödinger is the project of brothers Carlos and Ernesto Carapia, who mix post-punk, gothic rock and darkwave with delayed and reverberated guitars and synthesizers over cold, chaotic vocals. “International Decay” runs eight tracks: “Broken Cities,” “The Void,” “Ghost Nation,” “Eclipse of Faith,” “Metal Rain,” “Eleventh Hour,” “Caotica Penumbra” (featuring the Argentine gothic rock band Euroshima) and “Black Room.” International Decay by Schrödinger Schrödinger describe ‘International Decay’ as a more forceful record Schrödinger stated: “There’s a very noticeable change compared to the previous album. On the first album, we opted for a more minimalist sound, where space and atmosphere played a fundamental role, without losing that nocturnal identity that characterises the band. On this new album, there’s a clear evolution towards a more mature, solid and forceful sound. The compositions, arrangements and production were developed with a more precise approach, seeking greater depth, power and cohesion in each track. We believe it retains the essence of Schrödinger, but presents it with a more defined identity and a much more consolidated sound.” “Caotica Penumbra” features Euroshima, the Argentine gothic rock and darkwave band formed in Buenos Aires in 1986 by Fabián Iribarne, José Wyszogrod, Ricardo Parrabere and vocalist Wanda, whose album “Gala” was reissued on vinyl by Dark Entries Records in 2022. About Schrödinger Schrödinger formed in Mexico City around brothers Carlos Carapia (guitars, programming, synthesizers) and Ernesto Carapia (vocals, bass, electronics, synthesizers). After close to a decade of live activity, the duo issued their debut full-length, “Last Days on Earth,” in October 2020 through Swiss Dark Nights, an album built on the chaos of the human mind with reverbed, delay-heavy guitars over a dense, melancholic atmosphere. “International Decay,” released digitally on July 26, 2026 and following on vinyl and CD on September 4, 2026, is Schrödinger’s second studio album and continues the band’s work with Swiss Dark Nights.

items.body: US industrial metal band Black Magnet will play its first-ever Belgium show at Magasin 4 in Brussels on September 8, 2026, as part of the band’s first European tour. Tour dates for Black Magnet September 8, 2026 – Magasin 4, Brussels, Belgium Black Magnet plays industrial metal built on distortion, repetition and mechanized rhythm, citing Godflesh, Ministry and Nine Inch Nails among its reference points. The band will perform material from across its catalog on the tour alongside new, previously unreleased material making its live debut. The Brussels show is part of the band’s debut run of European dates. Megamantra by Black Magnet About Black Magnet Black Magnet started as the solo project of Midwestern US musician James Hammontree and has since expanded into a trio with the addition of Jared Branson and Ryne Bratcher, who also play with All Your Sisters, Destroyer Destroyer and Greg Puciato. The band released two albums through 20 Buck Spin before signing with Federal Prisoner, the label co-founded by artist Jesse Draxler and Greg Puciato of The Dillinger Escape Plan and Better Lovers, for its third album, “Megamantra,” released July 25, 2025. “Megamantra” was recorded at Earth Analogue Studio, engineered and mixed by Sanford Parker, mastered by Vlado Meller, and features additional synthesizers and background vocals by Eric Gorman. Black Magnet has toured as support for 3Teeth, Code Orange and Author & Punisher, and now returns to the road for its first European tour, which brings the band to Brussels for the first time on September 8, 2026.

items.body: Sorrow Stories, the project of UK artist Tina Forlorn, has released “So Sick”, her second collaboration with Christopher Hall of Stabbing Westward and The Dreaming, leading up to a full-length album planned for next year. Sorrow Stories and Christopher Hall’s ‘So Sick’ “So Sick” follows “Too Early [with Christopher Hall],” the pair’s first joint release, which came out on April 3, 2026, as an EP featuring remixes from Bow Ever Down, Null Device and Allie Frost. “So Sick” is described as the second track in the ongoing collaboration between Forlorn and Hall, with further material building toward a joint album. About Sorrow Stories Sorrow Stories is the project of UK artist Tina Forlorn, who writes, sings, produces, mixes and masters her own music across dark electro, darkwave, synthpop, EBM, industrial, alt-acoustic and soundtrack styles. Forlorn has self-released her work through Bandcamp since around 2009, after starting out with acoustic demos before moving into electronic production. Her soundtrack work includes music for the horror film “Swap,” released through Epic Pictures, and the short film “Tamesis Trilogy 1” with director Dennis Da Silva, which won the Jean-Luc Godard award for best experimental short in 2020. Sorrow Stories has previously collaborated with Aiboforcen on the 2024 album “Between Noise and Silence” and related EPs, with Aesthetische on the 2021 EP “Overflow,” and with Psy’Aviah on the “Bittersweet” album and its “Healing” and “Still Healing” EPs. Forlorn is currently working with Christopher Hall of Stabbing Westward and The Dreaming on new joint material, of which “So Sick” is the second release following April 2026’s “Too Early” EP.

items.body: French solo project Morphoex released the album “Méta Langages” on January 6, 2026, a 12-track record built around voices, field recordings and synthesizers, recorded on magnetic tape at a farm studio in Normandy. Méta Langages by MORPHOEX Morphoex’s ‘Méta Langages’ album “Méta Langages” is the seventh full-length released under the Morphoex name and the first to be almost entirely sung. The album is a concept record centered on voice, transmission and language, running as a continuous, uninterrupted listen. It includes twelve tracks: “Vagues sidérales,” “Schizodrome,” “Méta langages,” “Listen to the New Noise,” “Reality Is False,” “Tnemetohcuhc,” “Confuse Science Illustration,” “Black and White Lines,” “Vengeance Is Silence,” “Kinshasa,” “Toniki” and “Après un cataclysme.” Music and words are by Isthmaël Baudry throughout, except for “Schizodrome,” composed by Zaäk Årandi. Urban and nature sounds were captured through field recording, and the vocal and synthesizer parts were recorded onto magnetic tape at a studio set up on a farm in Normandy’s Eure department. Cédric Moglia recorded and mastered the album. About Morphoex Morphoex is the solo project of French artist Isthmaël Baudry, based in Rouen. Baudry also sings in the post-punk band Spleen XXX and in the project Love in Cage, whose track appeared in a Side-Line compilation. “Méta Langages” is Morphoex’s seventh album under the project name and its first mostly-sung release, following earlier releases including “An Imaginary Being.”

items.body: A pair of heavy hitting body music tours set to make their way across North America this fall ended up booking shows in Vancouver on the same day, and thankfully have been folded into one supercard, meaning that in a couple of months we’ll be getting to see Spike Hellis, Normal Bias, Buzz Kull, and Kontravoid all on the same night. A complete murderer’s row of modern EBM to be sure, but if you’re in NA you’ll likely have a chance to check out one if not both component parts as they’re extensive tours covering most of the continent. Hell, Spike Hellis is already on the road in support of the killer LP which finally dropped last week. Check the dates and grab tickets while listening to this week’s tracks. Are you Knormalled enough? Soft Vein, “Another Summer” Did you listen to our interview with Soft Vein on the podcast last week? If not, you should go do that right now, then come back here and listen to the exceptional “Another Summer”, yet another absolute stunner from the forthcoming All We’ve Known of Heaven. Justin Chamberlain’s songwriting, intimate style of performance and instrumentation keeps getting more undeniable with each release, and given the massive leaps he’s made in a mere three years, the overcast but beautiful skies are the limit for this melancholic LA based artist. One of our most hotly anticipated albums this year. All We've Known of Heaven by Soft Vein Patriarchy, “Bite Marks” Patriarchy are the enfants terrible of modern American darkwave, an act that provokes on stage and on record with each release. The thing is, the material backs it up, with last year’s excellent Manual For Dying showing off just how good the LA trio fronted by Actually Huizenga has gotten at bringing their gnarly stage show to their records. New EP Appendices is no different, featuring five tracks of mechanized shock rock and electro, expect to hear “Bite Marks” on your stompier dancefloors soonish. Appendices by Patriarchy Caustic, “Not Going Anywhere (Klack mix)” North American cult industrial impresario Matt Fanale follows up his last double LP Fiend with a remix album Unfiended, featuring a diverse roster of collaborators including Male Tears, Petrol Bastard, Alien Faktor, and Mark Pistel (!!!) amongst others. Of course Matt’s other project Klack dips in, bringing some of that new beat NRG to “Not Going Anywhere”, resolutely funky and full of more orch hits than a synclavier sample library. Giddy up! UNFIENDED by Caustic ner.ogris, “A View” German acts ner.ogris (or ner\ogris) have won us over via one LP and one EP of rock-solid electro-industrial which opts for considered grooves and sculpted sound design rather than shock or excess. This brooding taster from forthcoming LP Femme Fatale gets their strengths over quickly and artfully and bodes well for another course of proper home cooking from the pair. FAME FATALE by ner.ogris Knormalled, “The Servitor” The second EP from Indianapolis producer Knormalled shows a canny knack for a moody hybrid of dark electro and EBM which puts a premium on mood and slowly sliding timbral colour. Thru might best be appreciated as a full EP listen, but you can get a decent sense of the vibes from this shuddering slice. Should likely appeal if you’ve dug recent records by Kurs, or are still burning a candle for Distorted Memory. KNORMALLED THRU by Knormalled Ikon, “The Witness Tree” Some nice and easy summer goth rock from the always understated Aussie masters Ikon. Somewhat confusingly previewed then withdrawn, “The Witness Tree” is the first new material from Chris McCarter & co. in a few years and is setting up a forthcoming singles collection covering the entirety of the McCarter helmed era of the band. B-side’s got some dreamy pep, too. The Witness Tree single by IKON The post Tracks: August 10th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Band: Nostalghia | Album: Departure | Genre: Progressive metal | Year: 2026 From: Mexico City, Mexico | Label: Independent For fans of: Opeth, Enslaved, Riverside Bandcamp Nostalghia is a one-man project helmed by Mexican multi-instrumentalist Alex Becerra. This album is my first exposure to Nostalghia, but it looks like this is a very prolific project. According to RYM, this Departure is Nostalghia’s 14th release since their debut in 2020. The music on this record is stunningly diverse and ambitious. Aside from the band’s black metal roots, jazz, classical, alt-rock, classic prog, and more all play important parts here. “Leaving” opens the album on a restrained note. Acoustic guitar lines weave around one another in a way that draws from Baroque composers. When the vocals enter, they’re restrained. Rattling percussion, anxious strings, and tinkling piano build a sense of claustrophobia before suddenly cutting out and giving way to a melodic, piano-led passage that flows directly into the more-immediately-impactful opening of “Dearly Departed”. Riverside and Enslaved are both obvious influences in this song, with rapid, wiry guitar runs and vocals that vacillate between soulful and harsh. Latin jazz emerges about midway through as a nice bit of contrast. Many acts attempting such an incorporation come off as hokey and ham-fisted, but Nostalghia’s composition feels coherent and thought-out. The opening of “Uróboros” features some chamber music influence alongside restrained proggy folk, akin to acts like Jordsjø or Änglagård. When metal eventually emerges, there’s a wonderful, blistering solo supported by rich string arrangements. This sort of metal-classical hybrid is a not-uncommon trope in the realm of prog, but few acts pull it off this well. “Qa Muqu”, sung in a Mayan language and directly adapted from the Popol Vuh, has a peppy, jazzy opening. Enslaved-flavored black metal propels this piece along, with brass and piano exclamation points throughout. During instrumental passages, jazz once more comes to the forefront, and time signatures and rhythms get wonky as hell. The transitions between heavy and gentle moments are often sudden, but it all feels earned. Somber piano opens “Wherever You Are”. This is a mellow piece overall that gives the listener some appreciated breathing room. Riverside, Porcupine Tree, and Dream Theater’s better slow songs are all clear influences on this piece. “The Abyss Whispered” jumps back into metal, and tinkling chimes give it a celestial, otherworldly feel. The arrangements of the different parts of this song are diverse and complex, with some parts leaning into harsh black metal and others utilizing dissonant modern classical music. The final song on the album is the 10-minute “Offret (including “Ashes upon Eden”, “By the Corpse of Earth” and “Mercy”)”. “Ashes upon Earth” is led by clean guitar and pulls in elements of classical and dark folk music. I especially get flashes of some of Agalloch’s mellower output here. As distortion builds, so does the sense of majesty, before suddenly cutting out in the transition to “By the Corpse of the Earth”. Muted, atonal strings pluck and plink awkwardly and hauntingly, like the score to a horror film. Rattling chains and distant piano add to the ambiance. In the hands of less-skilled composers, this movement could easily become grating, but Becerra sells the tension and the anxiety. The final movement, “Mercy”, leans heavily upon ethereal atmospherics, with angelic vocals lifting everything skyward. Departure is a moving piece of music that displays an impressive breadth and depth of musical knowledge and skill. The songs demonstrate complex and technical instrumental ability, while the structures manage to be both diverse and coherent. The fusion of jazz and classical feels impressively natural, and I know there is a ton to discover upon repeated listens. Score: 92/100

items.body: The NWOSM (new wave of satirical metalcore) saw its resurgence with one band and one band only: Electric Callboy. I'm of the generation where hyper-energetic, Pixy Stix-snorting acts are either harshly condemned or praised to oblivion, and after I caught whiff of Electric Callboy's rejection to be the German entrant for the 2002 Eurovision Song Contest with the song "Pump It," I fell into a strict limbo. On one hand, I appreciated how the band took absolutely nothing seriously and still drew in tens of millions of views, but I deemed myself unready to earnestly listen to a full-length album of their uber-loud, electronic material. At the time, my adrenaline levels couldn't possibly handle the onslaught of cheesy choruses, the electronicore production, and the relentless attitude of the sextet. Fortunately, I've grown as a listener and as a reviewer, and Electric Callboy has given me a prospect to listen to fourteen whole tracks on their seventh LP, Tanzneid.Well, less than fifteen percent are truly brand-new. The final four pieces are remixes of both past and current cuts, with "Heartclub" and "The Savior" as the sole fresh songs. Singles for Tanzneid trace all the way to 2024–"Ratatata," featuring Babymetal, was released on the Tokyo-based, kawaii collective's latest record, already over a year old. The other singles create a timeline of anticipation, which is understandable given the context of modern marketing tactics, but it dilutes the ultimate impact of a new album releasing new music. In essence, Tanzneid isn't all that new.That doesn't mean the album isn't enjoyable, however. Its forefront focuses on hosting gimmicks, like Eurodance-infused breakdowns on the title-track, collaborations with established artists like The Offspring on "Let The Good Times Roll", pairings of wildly different styles, like rap metal/elevator music in "Elevator Operator", and tongue-in-cheek pop culture parodies, with Backstreet Boys-turned-deathcore number "The Way You Are" ironically being one of the harshest songs in terms of vocals, all situated closely together running order. Each piece achieves these merits within a digestible, radio-ready runtime and never comes off too farcical. Electric Callboy thrive in satire, meaning that weaker tracks—the ones that have no direct sonic gimmick—are unmemorable. These are shoved to the latter half of the album. The momentum doesn't hold for long though, sadly. At the halfway point, they begin instead to rely heavily on electronic metalcore that's comparably domestic compared to Callboy's rabidness. Even a duet with Frank Zummo of Sum 41 fame can't propel "Still Waiting" from the stretch of forgettability. When Electric Callboy abstain from silliness is when they start to chameleon themselves with the incoming waves of electronicore. "Heartclub," amongst other straightforward compositions, is unexpectedly brutal without any outside influence to contort its atmosphere, sitting in torpor amongst Scene-esque territories that the band supposedly ditched after their name switch. Tanzneid further overstays its welcome with some nine minutes of extra remixws, showing that they're still holding onto their past.I wouldn't mind hearing ten back-to-back gimmicks if it meant that Electric Callboy had freedom to poke fun at and experiment with as many styles as they please. It feels unorthodox to suggest that a band lean deeper into trivial, parodic themes, but for an entity like Electric Callboy who are already immersed in frantic craziness, I wanted to hear some truly hilarious music, with enough metal to mosh to. I chuckled, but guffaws were few across the multicolored brain of Tanzneid. This full album stream is like a compilation of the music videos. A mini-movie, of sorts.

items.body: 2026.08.11 NTT西日本のオープンイノベーション施設「QUINTBRIDGE」交流イベント 吹奏楽業界で近年、大きな課題とされている「部活動の地域展開」は、文科省の予算が圧倒的に不足していると言われるなか、現場の閉塞感が高まっている。吹奏楽部をどのように地域展開させるのか、そのアイデアを異なる業界の人たちと交流することで考えようというイベントが5月行われた。 和田響子 編集部 埼玉県出身。DTPや自転車など専門誌の編集部を経て、音楽之友社に入社。2015〜2022年3月に編集部のWeb担当として、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」やオンラインシ... 詳しく見る 部活動は2026年度からの6年間で「改革実行」へ 大阪市の京橋駅近くにあるオープンイノベーション施設「QUINTBRIDGE（クイントブリッジ）」。NTT西日本の本社ビルの敷地内に2022年に創設され、世の中をもっとよくしたいと考える人々が集い共創する場として、ワークショップやモノづくり、入居する会員の事業が行われている。 この「新たな出会いフロア」と呼ばれる1階で、5月15日、「部活動（吹奏楽）の地域展開を考える ― 地域と企業がともに描く、これからの“文化の支え方” 」と題するイベントが開催された。 部活動の地域展開とは 文科省が主導する部活動改革の一環。教員不足の原因のひとつとされる教員の長時間労働を是正するための「教員の働き方改革」に端を発し、「部活動のガイドライン」で活動時間などの制限について目安が提示されたうえ、公立中学校の部活動を教員に負担させないために、運営主体を地域（民間）に「展開」しようと各自治体が中心となって進められている。 すでに「改革推進期間」の3年間を終えて、2026年度から6年間の「改革実行期間」に入った。現状、休日については、過疎地域を中心に多くの地域で実施されはじめているが、平日に関してはさらに課題山積で、ごく一部の地域での実施に留まっている。 減少が危惧されている吹奏楽部の課題 吹奏楽部は、もっとも地域展開が難しい部活動とされている。 なぜなら、楽器や楽譜といった「備品」や、音出しが可能な「練習場所」は、学校部活動の練習環境だからこそ毎日のように使用できるものだからだ。学校の音楽室は、体育館のように独立した建物でない場合がほとんどなので、地域クラブの運営者が利用する場合は、セキュリティの問題を解決しなければならない。 また、吹奏楽にはおもに12種類の楽器があって、本来それらの指導ができる「専門人材」も必要だが、これまでは教員の献身的な努力を中心に、先輩が後輩を教える伝統的なスタイル、場合によっては外部講師を招くということで、何とか成り立たせてきた。 そのほか、コンクールや演奏会での「楽器運搬」費などもあり、活動費は運動部よりも高額になりがちだ。これまでは自治体からの補助金などで工面できていた部分があるが、地域展開して国や自治体の予算が不足している現状のままであれば、習い事の月謝と変わらない金額を受益者（保護者）が負担することになるだろう。そうすると、子どもが入部できるかどうかは親の判断にも左右されて、吹奏楽ができる子どもが限られてしまう。 こうした課題が横たわる吹奏楽部の地域展開だが、だからと言って、このままでよいという話にはならないだろう。急激な少子化により、1つの学校では合奏できる人数に満たない地域も増えているうえ、教員不足を解消するには働き改革が急務だからだ。 小中学校の団体数や部員数の減少を数字で説明 未来のクラブ活動の姿を民間の事業が提案！ さて、こうした課題に対して、QUINTBRIDGEのイベントでは民間企業、行政、学校の立場から、さまざまな解決案が提示された。筆者は後日に記録動画を拝見したのだが、どの登壇者もプレゼンテーションの熱量が高くて面白く、ポジティブに未来を捉えた発表だったことは、まず言っておきたい。 民間からは4人が登壇し、画期的なテクノロジーやサービスが紹介された。 まずは「離れていてもtonari（隣り）で過ごそう」というキャッチコピーで他のシステムと一線を画す遠隔コミュニケーションシステム「tonari」。床から天井までを映す大型スクリーン、タイムラグを感じることない通信技術、そしてカメラを意識せずに目線を合わせて等身大の相手と話ができるスクリーン内蔵型カメラを備える。吹奏楽の現場であれば、リモートでの指導や合奏が自然に行えるのではないかと期待が膨らんだ。導入コストの高さが課題だが、普及するのであれば、生徒の移動や楽器運搬の問題が解決でき、地域格差の是正につながるだろう。 NTT西日本グループからは、全国20以上の自治体と連携して社会実装を進めている自動運転EVバスが紹介された。山口県周南市では、2024年度から実証実験がはじまり、すでにNavya Mobility製の自動運転EVバスが街を走っていて、満車のことも多いという。バスやタクシーのドライバーの高齢化や不足を改善するだけでなく、生徒の移動手段として利用できる日も近いかもしれない。 そのほか、服部管楽器が学校にある「休眠楽器」を修理して格安にレンタルすることを検討していること、また、就活支援と企業の人事コンサルティングを行うHUB@LIFEが、「仕事ができる人に吹奏楽経験者が多い」と企業にアピールし、スポンサーになってもらいつつ学生とつなぐ場としてコンサートを開催していることを紹介した。 この日の登壇者を紹介するスライド 地域クラブを大人のバンドの下部組織に 学校や地域の現場からは、すでに動き出している事例として、まず西宮市立中学校の教員・吹奏楽部顧問が、外部に受け皿となる組織をつくった例が紹介された。 大人の吹奏楽団の下部組織に中学生対象のジュニアバンドをいくつかの地域につくり、当初から指導者を用意して演奏会など本番の予定も組み、活動をパッケージにして提示。これにより、生徒や保護者の活動への不安が軽減できたとのこと。 「どこかのジュニアバンドが縮小しても、バンドを統合したり、小学5年生から社会人まで入れる大人のバンドが受け皿になって、子どもたちの活動は守られる」と語った。前述したような吹奏楽ならではの課題はあるものの、指導者など大人たちのつながりによって支えられる好例となるかもしれない。 学校を「まち」に ！ 地域住民にも活動の場をつくる北海道安平町 自治体からは、北海道安平町教育委員会の教育長である井内聖氏がオンラインで登壇。安平町は人口は7000人ほど、小学校1校、中学校1校のほか、小中一貫の義務教育学校が1校あるが、子どもも大人も減り、スポーツ・文化に取り組む機会も減っている。この機会を支援するため、学校内に「まち」をつくった経緯や現状を語った。 安平町立中学校の部活動は令和7年度までですべて廃止にして、地域クラブの練習場所、時間、送迎、活動費については教育委員会が主導して調整を図った。地域おこし協力隊と総合型スポーツクラブが、スポーツ・文化活動の運営をサポートし、希望する指導者や教職員の兼職兼業によって指導者を確保。中学生だけでは成り立たないので、小学生から大人まで多世代のために環境構築を進めた。 このプロセスで、令和5年4月に義務教育学校として新設される予定だった安平町立早来学園をどのようにつくり、地域に開放するかが議論された。 この学校の空間デザインを担当したのが、デジタルアートのクリエイティブで知られるチームラボだ。顔認証によるセキュリティを導入するなど、テクノロジーを活用して、大中2つの体育館や図書館、家庭科室のほか、音楽室、美術室、技術室といった学校施設を、公民館のように地域とシェアし、ほぼ毎日9時から21時まで地域の人が簡単に利用できるようにした。 顔認証システムを導入し、地域住民が自由に出入りできる安平町立早来学園の図書館の様子が映し出された たとえば、平日の日中に学校内で、シニアの健康教室、子育て支援、料理教室などが開かれ、0歳から90歳が集うなか、休み時間には学校の子どもたちも本を借りに来る。昼休みに図書館で弦楽四重奏のコンサートを開き、シニアやお母さんと赤ちゃんといった地域住民に加え、先生、生徒が自由に集まり、食いつくように演奏を聴く――そんな自然に交流が生まれる光景も映像で紹介され、孤立や分断のない「まち」の姿の一つだと感銘を受けた。 吹奏楽部は今年度から地域クラブになり、この学校内で活動している。中心となる外部講師だけでなく、各楽器の講師も協力して指導にあたり、オンラインレッスンも活用している。今年は小学生1名を含む15名が所属。遠くから通う子どももいるため、平日16〜17時は自主練習、17〜19時で合奏などの全体練習を行い、保護者の理解も得ながら順調に活動しているそうだ。 ここに至るまでには、現場との意見の相違もあったそうだが、井内氏は「10年後のスポーツ・文化環境は、どうなっているだろうか」と関係者に問いかけ、「残すために」必要な形を模索していった。井内氏は、予測できない未来をどう予測するのか、「無理・難しい」の先にあるものは何か、それが吹奏楽がなくなるという未来であれば、私たちはそれを受け入れるのか――そう訴え、理解を得ようと努めたそうだ。 現状を変えることはエネルギーがいるが、まわりの変化が激しいなかで、何も行動しないことは逆にリスクになり得る。多くの地域住民が学校になごやかに集い、中学生だけでない多世代で多様なクラブ活動が行われている安平町の映像からは、この判断によって町全体の幸福度も高まったのではと感じられた。 オンラインで登壇した、北海道安平町教育委員会の井内聖教育長 財源を確保しながら、民間の力で魅力ある地域展開を 昭和の時代から続いてきた日本の部活動文化は、学校教育の一環としてその意義を評価されてきた。文科省の「部活動改革及び地域クラブ活動の推進等に関する総合的なガイドライン」（2025年12月）にもあるように、地域クラブになったとしても、その教育的意義は守っていくことが望まれている。 ただ、日本のスポーツ・文化や教育への投資が諸外国と比べても少なく、地域展開についても予算が不足している状況のなか、この改革の負担を現場の運営者や指導者、保護者に強いれば、スポーツ・文化は衰退してしまう（すでに小中学生の吹奏楽団体・人口は、明らかに減少している）。 公教育の一環として子どもの「機会均等」を守るためには、今回QUINTBRIDGEで発表されたような民間のアイデアを活用できるように、まず行政がしっかりと財源を確保しなくてはならないだろう。それが地域全体も活性化するような「魅力ある地域展開」に導くことになるのではと考えさせられる機会だった。 おカネがかかる芸術教育〜国際比較から考える日本の課題と活路

items.album: 全国の音高生が一堂に！21校、116名が参加した真夏の合同オーケストラ

items.excerpt: 2026.08.10 全国の音楽高校の学生が集まり、一つの音楽をつくり上げる「全国音楽高等学校合同オーケストラ演奏会」が、7月25日に東京の国立オリンピック記念青少年総合センターで開催。全国音楽高等学校協議会に加盟する62の高等学校のなかから、21校、116名が参加した。 道下京子 音楽評論家 2019年夏、息子が10歳を過ぎたのを機に海外へ行くのを再開。 1969年東京都大田区に生まれ、自然豊かな広島県の世羅高原で育つ。子どもの頃、ひよこ（のちにニワトリ）... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 初めての仲間と音を響かせる 全国から集ったメンバーは、それぞれの学校から推薦を受けた生徒。練習から本番までともに過ごし、一つのプログラムを創り上げていく。 指揮は現田茂夫。そして、コンサートマスターは、3曲それぞれ演奏順に東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校の本村菜々花、国立音楽大学附属高等学校の伊藤諒柊
items.body: 2026.08.10 全国の音楽高校の学生が集まり、一つの音楽をつくり上げる「全国音楽高等学校合同オーケストラ演奏会」が、7月25日に東京の国立オリンピック記念青少年総合センターで開催。全国音楽高等学校協議会に加盟する62の高等学校のなかから、21校、116名が参加した。 道下京子 音楽評論家 2019年夏、息子が10歳を過ぎたのを機に海外へ行くのを再開。 1969年東京都大田区に生まれ、自然豊かな広島県の世羅高原で育つ。子どもの頃、ひよこ（のちにニワトリ）... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 初めての仲間と音を響かせる 全国から集ったメンバーは、それぞれの学校から推薦を受けた生徒。練習から本番までともに過ごし、一つのプログラムを創り上げていく。 指揮は現田茂夫。そして、コンサートマスターは、3曲それぞれ演奏順に東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校の本村菜々花、国立音楽大学附属高等学校の伊藤諒柊、桐朋女子高等学校音楽科（男女共学）の田遠麗奈が務めた。 演奏会は、チャイコフスキー「幻想序曲《ロミオとジュリエット》」で始まった。低弦楽器がたっぷりと音を鳴り響かせ、ヴァイオリンなどがメロディをロマンティックに歌い上げる。続くモーツァルト《ディヴェルティメント》では、楽器ごとの親密な対話を生み出していた。休憩をはさんで、ベートーヴェン「交響曲第8番」。テーマやモティーフを丁寧に表わし、豊かな響きを作り出す。また、ハーモニーの変化に耳を傾け、音色を多彩に表現していく姿が心に残る。そして、音楽を次第に高揚させ、圧倒的なクライマックスを形成していた。 音楽高校は近年、少子化にともなって廃止されたり、オーケストラの授業が困難になっていたりするという。オーケストラ作品への取り組みや、その成果をコンサートホールで聴衆に披露した経験は、今後の彼らの活動に結びついていくに違いない。 若さあふれる熱演に、客席からは盛大な拍手がおくられた 公演データ 全国音楽高等学校合同オーケストラ演奏会 〈日程・会場〉7月25日・国立オリンピック記念青少年総合センター 大ホール 〈出演〉現田茂夫（指揮）、全国音楽高等学校協議会加盟校生徒 〈曲目〉チャイコフスキー「幻想序曲《ロミオとジュリエット》」、モーツァルト《ディヴェルティメント》、ベートーヴェン「交響曲第7番」

items.body: 2026.08.10 音楽祭に出かけよう！2026 毎年秋に東京・池袋の東京芸術劇場を中心に開催されている「サラダ音楽祭」（9/11-9/13）は、世代を問わず、誰もが楽しめるフェスティヴァル。オーケストラ、ダンス、歌を縦横無尽に味わうことができ、子どもの舞台デビューにもぴったりだ。今年から拡大されるメインプログラムや新企画など、色とりどりのラインナップをご紹介しよう。 文 文 飯田有抄 クラシック音楽ファシリテーター 1974年生まれ。東京藝術大学音楽学部楽理科卒業、同大学院修士課程修了。Maqcuqrie University（シドニー）通訳翻訳修士課程修了。2008年よりクラシ... 詳しく見る 誰もが楽しめる音楽祭 ［サラダ音楽祭 TOKYO MET SaLaD MUSIC FESTIVAL］は、2018年の開幕以来、東京・池袋の東京芸術劇場を中心に開催されている音楽祭だ。「サラダ」の由来は「Sing and Listen and Dance」の頭文字。その名のとおり「歌う、聴く、踊る」というコンセプトに重ねられた、フレッシュで彩り豊かなプログラム編成で、世代を問わず誰もが楽しめるフェスティヴァルである。 2026年の最大のニュースは、メインプログラムがこれまでの2日間から3日間へと拡大されることだ。初日9月11日の夜は、毎年フェスティヴァルの締めくくりを飾ってきた音楽祭メインコンサートが、祭典の幕開けへと据え直される。 東京都交響楽団を指揮するのは梅田俊明。仙台フィルハーモニー管弦楽団の常任指揮者を6年にわたって務め、国内の主要オーケストラへの客演を通じて、堅実かつしなやかな音楽づくりを聴かせてきた。メインコンサートの初登壇となる今回、その円熟した手腕がどのような響きを引きだすか、楽しみだ。新国立劇場合唱団の緻密で広がりある合唱と、金森穣率いるNoism Company Niigataの圧倒的で洗練された身体表現、そして都響とが立体的に織りなす公演となるだろう。 続く12日と13日には、0歳から入場できる「OK！オーケストラ」が両日開催へと拡張され、親子で楽しめるダンス公演「動物たちのダンス＆ミュージック」も新企画として登場。 さらに昨年好評を博した子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』も再演され、家族で味わえる本格的な舞台体験が広がる。SaLaDワークショップやアンサンブルレッスン、ヤマハと共同開発した「だれでもピアノ®」など、聴くだけにとどまらない参加型コンテンツの厚みも、この音楽祭ならではの特徴だ。 多摩・島しょ地域へと届けられる「OK！ オーケストラ in 多摩」や「SaLaDプレミアムコンサート」も今年さらに充実し、街と街、人と人、世代と世代をやわらかにつなぐ。秋の東京に、音楽の喜びが響き合う3日間がやってくる！ 音楽祭メインコンサート《Boléro》～ 音楽と舞踏の豪奢プログラム 好評の《ボレロ》は今年も目玉の一つ。華やかに名曲たちが奏でられる ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 「音楽祭メインコンサート《Boléro》」は祭典の幕開けを飾るにふさわしい、豪奢にして緻密なプログラム。指揮を執るのは梅田俊明である。NHK交響楽団や読売日本交響楽団など国内主要オーケストラと共演を重ねるヴェテランの登壇は、本音楽祭にとっても新たな色合いをもたらすに違いない。 昨年SaLaDプレミアムコンサートを指揮した梅田俊明が今年はメインを振る ©K.Miura 前半はグリーグ「組曲《ホルベアの時代より》」で北欧的な清冽さを響かせ、続くラター《グローリア》では、新国立劇場合唱団の輝かしい歌声が天井高くこだまするだろう。後半はラヴェル「組曲《マ・メール・ロワ》」が鮮やかなオーケストレーションで物語を紡ぎ、Noism Company Niigataとのコラボレーションが始まる。 そして、いよいよラヴェル《ボレロ》へ。サラダ音楽祭の象徴的演目ともなりつつあるこの演目は、Noism Company Niigataの舞踏が、凛々しく力強い身体表現で東京都交響楽団とのコラボレーションを展開する。希望や光を感じさせる音楽と舞踏の圧倒的世界に、聴衆は再び息を呑むことになるだろう。 OK！ オーケストラ～0歳から入場OK！ 家族みんなで楽しむ1時間 0歳から入場可能な「OK！ オーケストラ」では、指揮者体験コーナーも実施予定 ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 0歳から入場可能なオーケストラ・コンサート「OK！ オーケストラ」は、毎年大好評を博してきた人気プログラムだ。今年は土・日の2日間開催へと拡大される。タクトを振るうのは川瀬賢太郎。その伸びやかな音楽作りで、子どもから大人まで魅了する指揮者だ。司会には子ども向けTV番組でおなじみの小林顕作、ダンスは近藤良平率いるコンドルズ、児童合唱は東京少年少女合唱隊と、舞台はにぎやかな顔ぶれで埋め尽くされる。 指揮を担当する川瀬賢太郎は1児の父。「幼少期に本物の音に触れる体験の大切さ」をたびたび語っている ©Tomoko Hidaki プログラムもじつに贅沢だ。すぎやまこういち「交響組曲《ドラゴンクエストV》」から、ビゼー《カルメン》、ロッシーニ「《セビリャの理髪師》序曲」、シャブリエ《スペイン》まで、子どもも大人も心拍数が上がるような名曲がずらり。指揮体験コーナーや、客席も一体になって歌うコーナーもあり。声を出しても、身体を動かしてもOK！ 家族みんなで音楽の喜びそのものを体感する、かけがえのない1時間となるだろう。 子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』（日本語上演）～ 色鮮やかな冒険ファンタジー 『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』は自然と楽しめる曲が散りばめられており、子どもにも親しみやすいオペラとなっている ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 意地悪なトロールの女王に連れ去られたしろくまのヴァレモンを追って、心優しく勇敢な少女ラグナが冒険の旅へと踏み出す──昨年大好評を博した東京芸術劇場制作の子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』が再演される。 ヴァイオリン、クラリネット、トロンボーン、ハープ、打楽器という小さなオーケストラが、北欧の森や吹雪の山々を色鮮やかに描き出す。楽しく笑える場面も多いが、歌手たちの確かな歌、彩り豊かな照明、そして衣裳は、まぎれもなくオペラそのもの。子どもが新しい世界と出会い、大人が童心に帰る一時間である。 サラダ音楽祭2026 公式サイト
