items.body:
Avon’s lesser-hailed, glam ‘80s synth-pop and new wave movement is spotlighted in-depth via 20 songs compiled by studio engineer Dave Massey, who smartly portrays the breadth and quality of an ‘80s blindspot.

‘The Bristol & Bath Blitz Club Meets Art School Sound - 80's Explosion’ traces the reverberating influence of Rusty Egan and co.’s new wave crucible, The Blitz Club, along the M4 leyline, where it met Avon art school kids advancing from punk and funk into a new decade. Egan’s signature DJ brew - e.g. Kraftwerk to Visage, Burundi Black to Bowie, Japan and Grace Jones - would spark myriad emulators who were also mirroring the chops of Duran Duran (sons of the Brum club scene an hour north) and the likes of Martyn Ware et al in Sheffield, in their blends of US funk, European machine music, and a punky license to follow their nose. 

Fair to say it’s not the usual tale of Bristol’s dub-rooted and punk heritage. Between Distant Cousins’ Arabic-inflected new wave ace ‘Red Oasis’, and the angular chops of ‘Your Heart My Ambition’ from Frame By Frame, it checks for a spectrum of pop moxie taking in the swooning goth pop of Great Naked; BEF-meets-Bowie pomp of Wadi Vision; Nite Watch and glaxobabies’ disco-boogie; a stranger standout of synth sleaze by Startled Insects; Duran Duran-esque new wave funk by Creature Beat; and a ballad pearl by The Escape - all sure to mess with preconceptions of Bristol history.

items.body:
Key Chicago house architect Ron Trent departs the club for the bedroom under new alias La Marr, a new vent for his most romantic, sublime soundscapes, warmly advised FFO Detroit Escalator Company, Terre Thaemlitz, Wally Badarou, Klaus Schulze, MvO Trio

Light candles/incense and scatter petals for optimal effect when immersing in La Marr’s debut ‘Mood Programs’ EP, which finds a perfect home nestled amid Music From Memory’s precious, timeline-twining cuts of new age ambient, kosmiche, and Balearic wist. It’s also a natural, logical progression from the sort of depths usually secreted in Trent’s albums, but here given full sides to unfurl their functions, which we’re sure will also sound dead tasty, syrupy slow, on 33-not-45. 

He paints the lushest 12 min panorama of elliptical stereo pads, floating organ cloud structures and skin-stroke arps in ‘Good Magic’, edging on similar terrain to Terre Thaemlitz’s golden revision of Tangerine Dream’s ‘Love on a Real Train’, where a fine line of hand played drums emphasises the swaying groove - swooning either bed-ways or a little rug-cut, depending on your disposition - before ‘Clear’ hustles a palette of the slinkiest Afro-Latinate, Brazilian rhythms under big, dusky skies, hinting at Manuel Göttsching via MvO Trio. 

Your ears do not deceive you: this one is proper lush.

items.body:
jason calhoun’s fifth release for Dear Life Records,

"On revelations of divine love Calhoun has assembled an especially potent album of work that whirrs, hums, and glows. Unlike his recent output centered around extended, hypnotic compositions, the fourteen tracks here immediately request your attention and curiosity. Their concision only underscores one of his greatest strengths: the ability to capture an evaporating, fleeting moment, and hold it close.

The title is a nod to British Anchoress Julian of Norwich, whose collected writing of the same title is the earliest of any woman written in English. Here it serves as a unifying theme for Calhoun's particular palette of restless textures and tentative melodies. This is personal music, to be sure, but it also feels tactile, almost taffy-like in its presentation—and with such a potent combination, it is hard to resist a smile while listening. Like when the insistent pulse grounding 'last one' suddenly changes color as yawning tones reveal themselves, or how 'eye dilation' tiptoes into the room with each note sounding like a carefully chosen step. Though never precious or fussy, the album remains resolutely intimate.

Calhoun puts it plainly: “Julian of Norwich says “‘All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well’. These days, I’ve been having my doubts that this is true. As no solution to the issue at hand, I look for the revelations of divine love in my life, and I find them--in my partner asleep on the floor in our studio, my survival of a social interaction with a stranger, being bad at chess. Don't ask me what they mean-I'm still figuring that out myself. Maybe we can figure it out together.” It is from this place of doubt, searching, and openness that the album finds its footing."

items.body:
TTT tack to classical chamber music with the intimately fuzzy recital of richly melodic works written between mid-14th and 21st centuries and performed by NYC’s Cop Tears, a trio of early and avant garde music specialists; Derek Baron, Cameron kapoor, and John Andrew Wilhite.

Attending to an emergent TTT touchstone of recent times - as in Jack Sheen’s works, thru aspects of Will Bankhead’s What We and Guild mixes - Cop Tears lean into interests in quieter chamber music laced with threads of lo-fi, folk and jazz that tie ‘The Rules of the Game’ to the label’s key corpus. The 13 pieces follow five years from the trio’s ‘Theodor Adorno: Piano Works’, and five again from their debut ‘Thirteen Harmonies (1986) Selections From John Cage’s ‘Apartment House 1776’’, with enchanting slants on cherry picked pieces that endure, some over 600 years later, on the strength of their timeless arrangements.

In key with the label's thing, everything is swaddled in ferric gauze - possibly posited on auld tape recorders - and holds a peculiar, homely, discordant charm (including fits of giggles and room noise) for the duration, which never tests the patience. The C.14th, polyphonic chanson Ars Nova masterpiece of Guillaume de Machaut ‘Puis qu’en oubli’ is the set’s oldest, along with ‘Quam pulchra est’, a mid-C.15th work for recorder trio by John Dunstable, placed on the same page with the more angular chamber jazz modernism of ‘Selections from Piano Sonata after a Conversation with Jonathan Gean (2016)’ and their take on the naïf wooze of ‘Children's Music, No. 1, II: Modern Dance (1973)’ by Valentin Silvestrov. Our percy is the dreamy, creaking baroque elegance of ’S’io men vo (1618)’, but it’s best advised to take it all in one at your leisure...

items.body:
First re-pressing in years of Mark Ernestus & Moritz Von Oswald’s divine, final Rhythm & Sound release, heeling to tradition with a one-riddim album focussed on its carousel of roots reggae legends; Sugar Minott, Paul St. Hilaire, Willi Williams, Jah Cotton, Bobbo Shanti, and more

In 2005 Rhythm & Sound capped their holy mountain catalogue with ‘See Mi Yah’, a 7 x 7” set and LP which completed a 10 year run of inspired dub productions with their purest offering to the form. At the time, younger ears to their music would be left perplexed by the lack of instrumental variation - but any others with a little knowledge of one-riddim set traditions knew it was their ultimate ode to roots reggae fundamentals, after respectfully messing with the style & pattern across the Burial Mix 10”s (as collected in ‘w/ The Artists’), and the more radical 12” mutations of the Rhythm & Sound series, proper, since 1996 (not to mention birthing dub house-techno before that).     

Seeing off the project in fine style, Ernestus & Von Oswald gave studio time to their favourite vocalists, generating a slew of original performances displaying the range and depth of roots reggae’s elders and contemporary torch carriers on their signature backdrop of air-trodding bass and powdered dub chords. We were blessed to distribute it in the UK at the time, so many of these cuts are hard etched to the memory, from the ghostly croon of Willi Williams’ title piece thru the gruff gravitas of Bobbo Shanti, the duet between Ras Donovan & Ras Perez, and of course Sugar Minott’s mellifluous reggae soul.

In the year following ‘See Mi Yah’, Rhythm & Sound were naturally elected to edit and master a re-up of The Congos & Friends’ one-riddim album ’Fisherman Style’ for our then warehouse neighbours Blood & Fire Records, sealing their era of roots reflection by appropriately saluting the originators, in parallel to their Wackies reissue scheme, and before Ernestus (and Mark Ainley) would go on to found the more digi-devoted reissue label, Dug Out. Some 20 years of satisfaction later, time has proven this album holds its meditative weight.

items.body:
Lolina's back with an insouciant and uncharacteristically vinegary barrage of scandalous whispers that arrive dressed as a tribute to Gossip Girl, backed up with asymmetrical remixes from Arca and NEW YORK.

On 'gg', Lolina reminisces about broken dreams and heartbreak. "That's one secret I will never tell," she promises, over smudgy, time-stretched drums and muggy organs. "Let's get another drink, or do you think I should be sober for what I am about to say?" It's a sonic side-eye that may or may not be historical and the lore's only extended by the cryptic press release (provided by Kaitlin Simotics) and the two reworks of Lolina's original.

London duo NEW YORK channel Lolina's energy into pop, singing the refrain and beefing the casual charm up with an electroid bassline, while Arca heads off-world, using Lolina's puzzling narrative to inspire her most gaseous track since her run with Björk. Digital harps are interrupted with glitches, and Lolina's words are slowed against syrupy OPN-like chipmunked chorals that coalesce into a symphonic crescendo...

items.excerpt: To say that a work starts with a bang is a cliché, yet Boca De Acero definitely has an explosive intro. Not only that, the momentum on this five-movement duet remains taut till the final note. items.body: To say that a work starts with a bang is a cliché, yet Boca De Acero definitely has an explosive intro. Not only that, the momentum on this five-movement duet remains taut till the final note. A collaboration between two singular musicians, the Argentinian vocalist Ines Terra and Uruguayan guitarist Santiago Bogacz, this album is entirely improvised and demonstrates a seamless camaraderie between them. This abstract, cinematic conversation has a shifting mood and thrilling twists and turns within the underlying harmonic narrative. Track “1” opens with fiery, angular guitar strums and Terra’s wordless vocal acrobatics. Terra makes her shouts and cries bounce off Bogacz’s strings with dramatic flair. The guitarist weaves a dense and dynamic soundscape around Terra’s chants. [Text Wrapping Break]Despite embracing dissonance, the pair maintains a subtle lyricism throughout their exchanges. The darkly hued “2” brims with mysticism. Terra’s rising and falling voice hauntingly floats over Bogacz’s sparse chords. The refrains that evolve with each repetition have a ritualistic feel, almost like the ceremonial liturgy of a long-forgotten ancient rite. With “3” the somber mood continues, becoming quieter and more nocturnesque. Terra softly whispers, and Bogacz plucks single notes that underscore the serenity of the mood. Their conversation takes on a sublime theatricality. Meanwhile, on “4” the two artists fully embrace mysticism as her throat singing and his hypnotic strums ebb and flow against a quiet backdrop, ending on a passionate note. The fifth piece features synthesizer sounds that distort the emotive and stimulating improvisation, creating a delightfully otherworldly atmosphere. The burgeoning piece melds the organic quality of the human voice with sharp, acerbic electronic vamps for a performance that is simultaneously stimulating and eerie. With Boca De Acero, Terra and Bogacz have undertaken a successful sonic experiment that is provocative and moving. It is also a much-needed glimpse into South America’s vibrant improvisational scene. That, much like the recording’s creators of this album, is unique, expressive, and fearless. Boca de acero by Inés Terra + Santiago Bogacz Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.excerpt: 今年、生誕100周年をむかえたマイルス・デイヴィス。マイルスについて書かれた本が数多く世に出たけれど、これほどまでに彼の音楽の中身にフォーカスされたものは他にない。アルバムごとの演奏を事細かに分析し、マイルスの即興演奏への向き合い方の変容を捉えることで、ジャズミュージシャンとしてどのように新しいものを生み出そうとしていたのかが浮き彫りになる。また、ライヴの映像での仕草やアルバムとのセットリストの違いなど音の外側にも目を向け、彼の思考に迫ろうとしているのが面白い。やや音楽に精通した人向けの内容ではあるものの、マイルスの音源を聴きながら楽しんでほしい一冊である。

items.body: Label: UnderPool, 2026 Personnel - Anggie Obin: flute; Bill McHenry: tenor saxophone; Miguel “Wiwi” Garcia: piano; Masa Kamaguchi: double bass; Estefania Chamorro: drums. Rising Panamanian jazz flutist and composer Anggie Obin, who attended Berklee College of Music in Boston and is based in Barcelona, gathers a first-class quintet—American saxophonist Bill McHenry, Cuban pianist Miguel “Wiwi” Garcia, Japanese bassist Masa Kamaguchi, and Spanish drummer Estefania Chamorro—for a wonderful debut album that honors her musical mentors and her late great-grandmother. Luz was titled after the latter, an important pillar in her life. “ For Mr. G ” begins the album in warm modal complicity, with saxophone and flute beautifully interlocking through contrasting timbres. The piece, dedicated to saxophonist Carlos Garnett—with whom Obin first recorded professionally—features her wandering freely, choosing exquisite, breathy notes with spotless intonation that makes us search as much as she does. There’s also catchy melodic input from McHenry, who captures Coltranean vibes in his solo, while Kamaguchi showcases the foundational sophistication for which he is known. “ Flash of the Spirit ”, a grateful nod to versatile bassist Santi Debriano, evolves with playful hard-bop flair, bluesy chops, and hints of Monk’s music. The quintet swings and grooves, revolving around freshly introduced ideas and a modern jargon that still drinks from the wells of tradition. Here, Obin is highly conversational in her statement, sounding as radiant as she does on “ Luz ”, where a delicate rubato introduction takes an emotional turn into a charming 3/4 drive. Obin’s expression is remarkable, Garcia’s measured piano playing comes wrapped in modal alchemy, while McHenry navigates abstract alleys of his own imagining. “ La Eucaristia ” exudes solemnity and dark contours through its leaping angular melodies, featuring an exchange of rapid motifs between Obin and McHenry. If the that piece was inspired by experimental multi-instrumentalist Anthony Braxton’s work, then the mercurial “ Ballot or the Bullet ” is a blues inspired by human rights activist Malcolm X’s speech. Obin kills it with soulful tones and brilliant technique. Recorded live at Estival de Jazz d’Igualada in Spain, Luz emphasizes the elasticity and potential of each composition, leaving a lasting impact. Obin’s highly attuned quintet cuts through modal post-bop and Panamanian roots with superb fluidity, providing an immersive listening experience. Favorite Tracks: 01 - For Mr. G ► 02 - Flash of the Spirit ► 04 - Luz

items.body: After the void on a distant sun (2023) and [limen memoriae] (with Luca Ferro, 2024), Angelo Panebianco and Matteo Mariano return as phoanøgramma with dream flow, a single long-form composition presented in six movements. Although divided into individual tracks for navigation, the work was conceived as an uninterrupted whole, with the titles reading like successive lines of a single poem. From beginning to end, the music remains in constant motion, continually altering density, and texture without ever interrupting its flow. Panebianco establishes the broad harmonic terrain with slowly expanding drones, while Mariano introduces subtle perturbations that keep the surface in perpetual motion. “raindrops (prelude)” begins with rhythmic droplets that gradually dissolve into bubbling textures as broad circular harmonies gather around them before acquiring an insistent metallic edge. “arise in sinking feelings” darkens the atmosphere, introducing currents of unease that quietly unsettle the calm established at the outset. “fractures” opens onto an immense glacial space where deep resonances stretch into the distance while minute electronic activity continues beneath them, gradually generating a dense web of interacting signals. The balance shifts during the second half. “where things are hollow” allows machine-like chatter and electronic circuitry to emerge with increasing clarity before they slowly sink back into the surrounding drone during “a cecasting of indices”. By the closing chapter, “the vanishing”, the droplets heard at the beginning quietly reappear, completing the album’s circular trajectory. Repetition, rotation and inversion shape the work throughout, with recurring materials returning in altered forms as though recalled from memory rather than simply repeated. The six chapters reveal a compositional practice built on serial procedures, recurring materials and gradual transformation. Sounds return altered by context, textures migrate from foreground to background, and seemingly incidental details quietly reshape the listener’s perception of what came before. The result is an album whose continuity arises from the way each recurrence subtly modifies the whole. To guide us through the different undercurrents of the album, Angelo Panebianco and Matteo Mariano have agreed to answer four questions by email. phoanøgramma’s previous releases, from the void on a distant sun to [limen memoriae] — with Luca Ferro — often seemed concerned with memory, distance, thresholds and liminal states. dream flow feels like a continuation of those interests, but also a more fluid and immersive work, unfolding almost as a single dream process rather than a collection of discrete compositions. How do you see this album in relation to your earlier collaborations, and what new territory were you trying to explore together here? You have certainly identified one of the central intentions behind the album: the idea of fluidity and immersion. In this sense, we see this last album as an evolution in terms of intention. Our previous works were also connected to ideas of memory, distance, thresholds and unstable spaces, but they were based on more abstract or suggested concepts. With dream flow, the concept was not only a background suggestion, but a real compositional direction: we wanted to evoke a specific condition, a circumscribed but open-ended image — the continuous transformation of perception inside a dream, in which everything moves continuously, changes shape, dissolves and reappears without clear boundaries. Musically, we also wanted to move toward a more classically ambient/drone form. the void on a distant sun had darker moments, with a strong presence of tapes and synthesizers, while [limen memoriae] had a dimension closer to improvisation and electroacoustic interaction. For dream flow, we worked in a more programmatic way, starting from the concept itself and shaping the material accordingly. It is probably a more carefully studied work, less instinctive in its construction, even though we wanted to preserve the sense of instability and suspension that belongs to the dream state. The title dream flow and the accompanying text suggest a work built around transformation, dissolution and the unstable logic of dreams: “fractures bloom where things are hollow” and “a recasting of indices spirals toward the vanishing.” Were these tracks shaped by specific dreams, subconscious imagery and personal experiences, or are you more interested in creating the conditions under which listeners can project their own dream narratives onto the music? There is certainly a personal inspiration behind dream flow, coming from our own memories of dreams and dreamlike states. One example is the cover image itself, which represents an imaginary environment where sky and earth seem to exchange places. That image was suggested by a childhood dream remembered by Matteo: he was swimming in a lake, looking up at the sky, and beyond the clouds he could see mountains, almost as if he were looking down from above. Of course, it is impossible to translate such an image directly into music. What we tried to do instead was to start from our own personal images and memories, but without turning them into a closed narrative. We wanted to create a sound environment in which the listener could enter freely, bringing their own dream memories and associations into the experience. So the album is not meant to describe a specific dream in a literal way. It is more about creating the emotional and perceptual conditions for a dreamlike process to take place — something that can carry the listener from the beginning to the end, while leaving enough space for their own inner images to emerge. Both of you come from slightly different backgrounds and working methods. Matteo’s recent work on albums such as Magnetic Series explored the materiality and constraints of tape manipulation, while Angelo’s solo work as Phoan often embraces intuition, spontaneity and the search for hidden sounds within sounds. How did those approaches intersect during the making of dream flow? Was the album built through careful composition, improvisation, sound design, or some combination of all three? Having two different ways of working, and two different ways of approaching sound, was actually one of the strengths of the project. At times our methods can seem quite distant from one another, but this distance allows each of us to contribute where we feel more naturally effective. In the case of dream flow, Angelo brought the initial structure of the work and much of the raw drone material that runs through the whole album. Matteo’s role was more connected to a later stage of manipulation and construction: taking the material generated by Angelo and working on it in a more architectural way, assembling, reshaping and refining the overall form. So the album was born from a combination of intuition, sound design and careful composition. The intuitive element was essential in generating the first material and discovering the hidden qualities within it, but the final shape of the album came through a more deliberate process of editing, transformation and structural control. We were interested in preserving the organic nature of the original sounds, while giving them a clear long-form direction. The album is presented as six separate tracks with a continuous mix. Listening to it feels less like moving from one composition to another than drifting through different states within the same dream. Indeed the track titles read like verses from a single poem. How did you approach shaping that long-form narrative? Were you thinking in terms of tension and release, recurring motifs, or even something closer to cinematic editing, where one scene dissolves into the next without a clear boundary? We approached the album as a single long-form piece divided into six moments, rather than as six fully separate compositions. The track division gives the listener a possible map, but the real form of the album is the continuous flow. In shaping that flow, we were probably closer to the idea of cinematic editing than to a traditional sequence of individual pieces. We were interested in transitions, dissolves, changes of density and perspective — the way one sound environment can slowly become another without a clear boundary. In a dream, scenes often change in this way: you do not always perceive the exact moment of transformation, but suddenly you find yourself somewhere else. There are forms of tension and release, but not in a dramatic or narrative sense. They are more connected to perception: expansion and contraction, presence and distance, saturation and emptiness, moments of greater density followed by more suspended or rarefied passages. Some materials and gestures return, but often in altered forms, as if they were memories of something already heard rather than clearly recognizable motifs. The choice of titles also follows this idea of a fluid dream state. Each title can be read individually, as if it framed a specific moment or image within the dream, but the titles can also be read in sequence, almost as a single poetic line that describes the entire oneiric process. In that sense, they are not simply names for separate tracks, but fragments of the same movement. For this reason, we considered it very important to present the album as a continuous mix. This was also taken into account for the physical CD edition: the album is conceived as a single uninterrupted flow, divided into individual tracks that function more as indices of a whole than as autonomous pieces. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: From noise to nice. Harsh to honed. Squelch to sculpture. Ectospasm is a 10/10 top-tier proposition for anyone still prepared to leave the comfort of the known and go poking around in whatever is moving about underneath it. Stomping through a distorting ping and brace-breakbeat Ectospasm by Myoptik   Now that’s more like it. Production pushed deeper into the exploratory, the exploratory pushed deeper into the production, atmospheres absolutely everywhere on Myoptik‘s latest drop Ectospasm. Eight experimental sculptures, two of which are, for reasons that remain gloriously inexplicable, fifteen-minute attention-stretching time-space continuum-ripping mind-warping rational-pondering joy events, taking us somewhere between possibility and potential while making a quite deliberate decision not to run with the pack. Which is probably why, by the time we emerge, we are unequivocally not the same creation that pressed the first triangle and set track one loose. There is parasitic dalliance via opener “Framez v4.” Breaks. Squelches. Drum with bass, drum without bass, things behaving like drum and bass while being absolutely, defiantly, not drum and bass. That’s not drum and bass. Later, malfunctioning ambience a​rrives with the express intention of making relaxation impossible. Big fat industriana follows, metal-bashing its way through both form and formlessness, while the machinery seems increasingly uncertain about whether it is machinery at all. Then comes the epic whale of time that is “Dirt stoP Pt2″—and yes, that very awkward capital P is a tell—stomping through a distorting ping and brace-breakbeat, vocal treatments twitching at the edges while bubbling synths disappear down some kind of mycelium reverie. It’s enormous. It’s odd. It takes its time. It does not apologise for any of this. The first of our fifteen-minute treats is the caterwauling, mind-expanding throwdown of “Dungeon Stalker E,” a thing that thrashes your backside onto the floor and then protests at every subsequent attempt to stay still. And this, folks of all genders, is where those with enough gall—or precisely the right concoction of consciousness—to keep up for its full duration may well have attained legendary status. Absolutely wicked belter of a tune. The kind that turns up halfway through a collection and suddenly puts the whole damn thing in my top ten of the year. Spanking, dog-down-deep, dirty shizzle. A proper monster. Completely bent-out-of-shape genre-hybridizing :: And somewhere across all this glorious disobedience is perhaps the most diverse, inclusive and completely bent-out-of-shape genre-hybridizing archetype for modern times you’re likely to encounter. Ectospasm doesn’t just blur the boundaries between genres; it seems to regard the boundaries themselves as an outdated administrative error. Everything gets invited. Everything gets mangled. Everything gets a turn. Breakbeat, noise, ambience, industrial, squelch, electronics and whatever else happens to wander into the room are thrown into the same beautifully dysfunctional ecosystem and left to figure out their own relationships. And that’s really the thing with Ectospasm. It routinely refuses to play the game. It doesn’t seem particularly interested in familiarity, conformity, genre obedience or that increasingly tedious practice of self-aggrandising pastiche where the safest way to sound new is apparently to sound exactly like the people you already know. This is not lazy music. It is music working. Properly working. Working at the listener. Working on the listener. Working hard enough to create the possibility of something happening that wasn’t already there when you pressed play. And because of that, it is absolutely full of potential. From noise to nice. Harsh to honed. Squelch to sculpture. Ectospasm is a 10/10 top-tier proposition for anyone still prepared to leave the comfort of the known and go poking around in whatever is moving about underneath it. Ectospasm is available on Zoku – Zoku. [Bandcamp] Ectospasm by MyoptikThe post Myoptik :: Ectospasm (Zoku – Zoku) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Potato.exe executes precision-built, acrobatic sound structures that, despite their mechanical framework, still exude warmth through rhythmic foundations of remarkable control. A study in disjointed layers connecting The vast and expensive field of glitched-out microbial electronics takes full form as Potato.exe pulls from every angle on ERR_SESSION VOL.1, released through the ever-forward-positioned Clean Error imprint. Opening with a barrage of video-game clicks and cuts, delicately woven blips give way on “Pxlrn” to explosive breakbeat strata, while “Tlrnc.0” and “Plk3rn” maneuver through mechanically shaved and articulated rhythms. Less a collection of disheveled pieces than a study in disjointed layers connecting, the record gradually reveals complex and creative broken-electro-nic forms. Highlights “Trsh_Lp” and “Glnch.v2” take shape through morphing, Autechre, Alva Noto, and Suumhow-shaped crevasses, as Potato.exe generates several miles of crunched, sound-scraping beats on this inaugural ERR_SESSION series. “Vctr_∅∅” dives deeper into rugged terrain, opening up experimental avenues without losing its focus. This downtempo foray into glitch and grit closes with the head-bobbing final chapter, “Klmn0,” bringing everything together in one fell swoop of cohesive flutter. items.body: Rather than simply calling out for someone to remain, Geyzel uses these five tracks to explore what happens when you finally stop holding everything in. Its hidden strength is found in that openness: a willingness to wander through uncertainty, sit with absence, and ultimately let it all out. Stay. opens into a more vulnerable space Five tracks make up Serge Geyzel’s Stay. EP, revealing a different side of the multi-talented Saratov, Russia and Berlin, Germany-based sound sculptor. While analog gear and synthesizer production remain firmly at its core, this release opens into a more vulnerable space, where emotion slowly rises through ambient passages and drifting acoustic waves, as heard on the opening title track. Geyzel’s sleek electronic instincts are still present, but Stay. takes a looser, more exploratory route, moving through downtrodden jazz, hip-hop breaks, and fractured rhythms. “Some of It I Am Not” seems to unravel in fragments, gathering scattered thoughts and feelings along the way. As the EP unfolds, “But Then I Met You (for SF)” carries that wandering, Teebs-like sensibility into more uncertain territory, its searching quality sounding almost like a message sent toward someone, something, or perhaps life and love itself. Closer “Let’s Continue from the Beginning” feels like a long-lost sibling to that sentiment, bringing the journey full circle without quite resolving it. The penultimate “Pseudonostalgia” is perhaps the EP’s quietest revelation. Cruising under the radar, it evokes the strange sensation of remembering ​an event you never actually experienced—something unfolding somewhere deep in the background, half-formed and difficult to place. Acoustic instruments, samples, and distant voices gradually shed layers of melancholy, giving the piece a ghostly sense of memory. The liner notes describe the emotional distortion of time that comes with missing someone, particularly when longing for their return. That feeling sits at the heart of Stay. Rather than simply calling out for someone to remain, Geyzel uses these five tracks to explore what happens when you finally stop holding everything in. Its hidden strength is found in that openness: a willingness to wander through uncertainty, sit with absence, and ultimately let it all out. Stay. is available on Bandcamp. Stay. by Serge GeyzelThe post Serge Geyzel :: Stay. EP (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Luca Young crafts a hypnagogic birthing enclosure in the space created by this music, a space open for manifesting further gifts of reflective imagination. A sun shower appears, a brief trickle of luminescent moments Infinite Lovers, Pt. I by Luca Young   Electric guitar glitch swims in out of phase and out of focus photographs recovered from a forgotten SD card on the first song, “Welcome to the Other Side.” It reminds me of the skipping CDs used by the likes of Oval, clicks stuttering over top of field recordings of what sound like an airport or train station (a place of departure and return). It’s arrival music from the place we’ve departed from. These mesmeric textured loops are structured around they hypnotic guitar lines, themselves looping. All cascade and oscillate into the fog of timbral static coming off the Pacific. A disconsolate chord bathed in tape hiss and pitch shifted down starts “Pygmy Song.” The listening mind is teased by moments of reversed loops and the slide of fingers across the strings while glassy electronics appear for brief seconds in moments of fragility. Voices in staccato are cut and chopped alongside noisy high pitched tones who never overstay their welcome. It’s the music of dream memory trying to be captured and held onto, slipping away before it is fully grasped. On “7073” pensive upbeat strings meet with bo​uncing ball sounds and echo effects before swimming into crystalline pools of translucent electro refraction. Sounds of wave release the surf to the shore, and liquid textures. Small schools of musical fish swarm together for a moment, then separate in the drift of gentle abstract pulses and beats, the glitter of tiny notes surfacing for a second and then disappearing back into the deep. A sun shower appears, a brief trickle of luminescent moments. Directing the awakening of energy at the base of the spine :: The sound of planes rising or descending and further airport like sounds merge in a miasmic gloop at the beginning of “Kundalini.” The woman’s voice over the loudspeaker is comforting, directing the awakening of energy at the base of the spine, third eye subtly tingling by the luminescent vibrations. Further voices seem to be run through a gated sequencer, garbled through formant filters, language reduced to phonemes in a downtempo melodic style then disappears along the drift of a smoothly changing line. Infinity is in the distance. Part I of Infinite Lovers ends with the fifth track, “Ethiopia.” It’s starts with the ripple of tinkling pianos before building up successive pressure with louder playing, swoops of textural noise, warbling sonic transformations, glitch patterns, and long sweeps of filled with emotional grain. On this release Luca Young “was stepping into new territory artistically, moving away from a previous project. I decided to release this music under my given name, shedding an old artistic identity. It felt like the right move — a more honest expression of the kind of music I wanted to make.” The music is honest and unpretentious, warm and inviting. Leaving the skin of the old projects behind, he takes the listener on a voyage to the other side. It will be exciting to hear what comes with Part II. Infinite Lovers, Pt. I is available on Lōʻihi. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The serial production aimed to expose the artifice behind the image, a concept applicable to any work conveying an underlying message. In this instance, it is music... which, through repetition, reveals itself to be more than it initially appeared. The cover of Taking Tiger Mountain (By Strategy) offers a clue as to what is going on. Several things happen simultaneously. Eno's calm vocals on "Burning Airlines Give You So Much More" head in one direction, while the guitars perform a different function; they are superimposed layers, much like Andy Warhol's serial-style photographs. The repetitive modal texture is merely the starting point for this game of Chinese boxes, which, when opened, reveal something different, something new. Something about "Back In Judy's Jungle" reminds me of those strange pop songs by 60s psychedelic bands, tracks with a circus-like atmosphere, such as Pink Floyd's "See Emily Play.""The Fat Lady of Limbourg" is more futuristic, closer to Krautrock and quintessentially Eno, featuring the songwriting style and vocal approach that remain constant regardless of the musical vehicle. After all, there is the playful, simpler Eno, or rather, a simplicity that emerges from complexity, and the openly experimental Eno, with echoes of Roxy Music in the mix. The track features electronic effects and Andy Mackay on saxophone, sounding like the wind-instrument simulators Eno would use later in his career (on Nerve Net, 1992), which once again interrupt and fracture the tempo. Nothing here is quite what it seems.Mother Whale Eyeless features Phil Collins on drums, a longtime friend of Eno who, at the time, was eager to collaborate on any experimental project that came along. Their experimental sensibilities meshed well, allowing them to find the spaces to transform the drums into yet another melodic instrument; they introduced variations that added color and diverse pitch ranges to the track, complementing the work done on guitar, given Phil Manzanera's presence throughout the album. Polly Eltes' guest vocals enhance those aforementioned higher registers... especially since the bass line later brings the pitch back down.The Great Pretender returns with dark Krautrock; we give thanks for the 1975 setting and the era of Eno's "albums", records that did more than just scratch the surface or float aimlessly, instead digging deep to reach new horizons, even when those horizons lay in unexpected places. Robert Wyatt handles percussion and Phil Manzanera plays differently, distorted, just as Eno sings differently: in a deep voice, enunciating deliberately, and slowing down his guitar, which seems to ooze as if made of fuel."Third Uncle" seems to begin with Roger Waters' bass, but Brian Turrington (who had previously played with Manzanera on Diamond Head) quickly launches into a tour de force, a race against time, while the Roxy Music guitarist does what he does best: transporting us from the known world to another dimension or universe, without spaceships or artificial substances, relying solely on the power of the mind and the act of listening. The composition was, of course, Eno's work; he adds weight to the notes and accelerates his vocal delivery, bordering on rapping, while the bass and guitar keep pace with his rapid-fire style, creating a true sonic experience. He would later elicit a similar approach from The Edge on U2's Zooropa, an album Eno was also involved in.The Portsmouth Sinfonia handles the strings on "Put A Straw Under Baby", a sound that is somewhat symphonic and childlike, yet also evokes a dockside atmosphere, with a deliberately nomadic feel. Vocal groups play a pivotal role on "Taking Tiger Mountain"; Randi & The Pyramids join Eno on "The True Wheel," creating a strange, postmodern pop-soul sound that even veers into punk and, thanks to Manzanera, experimental territory."China My China," once again featuring Robert Wyatt, sets out to subvert standard time signatures, incorporating atonal guitar work and the sounds of typewriters, alongside funky guitar lines.The title track closes the album; it is almost an elegy, one of those melancholic odes that are quintessentially Eno. Indeed, this is an album containing many Enos, and each distinct version faithfully represents the original. Yet there is no single original; there are many. There is the Krautrock Eno, the Fusion Eno, the Psychedelic, the Electronic, the Art-focused, and the Simple Eno, the latter being the persona he always chooses for his farewells, promising to return with a soul chorus that touches the very soul.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is a piggy bank here, and inside it lie precious treasures, such as the debut of one of the great voices: that of Francesco Di Giacomo.The first of the coins stored within is the track titled "R.I.P." (Requiescant In Pace); here, Renato D'Angelo (bass) and Marcello Todaro (guitar) adopt a jazz-infused style, playing with a rhythm and speed that transcend the composition itself, revealing their sheer eagerness to play. While Gianni Nocenzi plays the piano, his brother Vittorio Nocenzi delivers a solo that straddles the line between psychedelia and the Canterbury scene. This very special piggy bank holds coins with two sides, and even three (thanks to that third dimension). That is why the piano takes on a classical tone, mirroring the vocals of Francesco Di Giacomo, a voice destined to be unforgettable from the very first moment you hear it.Passaggio features a harpsichord played by Vittorio Nocenzi; how could one not be captivated by this second "coin", small, yet equally valuable and memorable?Metamorfosi is that elusive coin, kept despite being worn and of dubious origin, whose relief is bold enough to carve out a place in the collection through the sheer force of its hammering piano, like a suite for tails and piano... yet it then mutates, hence the name, into an underground adventure where guitar and organ forge a path through subway tunnels. It is astonishing when the organ takes over the bass lines and the instruments swap roles, all held together by Pier Luigi Calderoni, who constantly shifts rhythms on the drums. When Marcello Todaro enters, he plays with wild, piercing intensity on the electric guitar, while the piano continues with classical scales. This is what should be shown to anyone wanting to experience progressive rock at its peak, music that was once new, wild, and unexpected, and which remains so to this day.Il Giardino Del Mago is the fourth coin... its origin is undetermined, no one knows how it got there, yet it is the oldest and most valuable. It is carved into four parts, with its faces divided. After some choral passages, a hard-rock sound erupts, accompanied by organ, reminiscent of early Deep Purple in its wildness, were it not for the heavily dramatic, operatic, and Mediterranean elements.The second side picks up the pace; the organ, piano, and guitar are just as important as Francesco's tenor voice. In "Chi Ride E Chi Geme," the Emerson, Lake & Palmer-style rush pauses to give way to a section reminiscent of Pink Floyd, evoking Obscured by Clouds, though only until the piano shifts into a classical mode... and everyone joins in singing. Marcello Todaro also features on the third side, with Gianni Nocenzi playing the clarinet as an ancient, distinctly Italian melody blends with progressive rock."Compenetrazione" represents the final side of the coin, where an acoustic guitar heralds the beginning of the end. Such a refined composition is hardly surprising for a 1972 debut, it is a track held in especially high regard. "Traccia" serves as the classical coda they would revisit from time to time, almost a private anthem the group kept for themselves. It is sung by the sextet in a spirit of communion akin to a secret society, a ritualistic bond that seemed to guarantee artistic success.

items.body: Review by OlyaBeginner — Listening to 'Never for Ever' felt like entering a strange emotional and almost theatrical world. I am not an expert in Kate Bush's music, so I approached the album mostly through my own feelings, images, and associations. What impressed me most is how freely she plays with her voice which becomes almost another instrument.1. BabooshkaA very playful and energetic song with a bright sound that immediately sparks emotions. There is something almost mischievous about it. At first, the music feels light and catchy, but underneath it there is a rather bitter and complicated story about love, jealousy, and mistrust. I really like this contrast between the almost cheerful sound and the darker emotions behind it.2. DeliusThis song is very strange and mysterious, but in a beautiful way. It creates an almost magical atmosphere, as if the listener is entering another world. The sound feels peaceful but also slightly unreal. It elevates the soul to another level and leaves me with the feeling of being somewhere far away from ordinary life.3. Blow AwayMy favourite song on the album. There is such an interesting play with Kate Bush's voice here. She seems to move between different emotional states, and the song feels almost theatrical. It charges me with energy while making me feel something tragic and elevated at the same time. There is a strange combination of excitement and sadness that I find incredibly beautiful.4. All We Ever Look ForA very strong song with a lot of emotional power. It feels as if it can touch something deep inside the listener. To be honest, I did not understand the meaning of it at first. After thinking about it more, I see it as a song about family, inheritance, and the things people spend their lives searching for. We inherit things from our parents, leave the family home, and then continue searching for love, security, meaning, or something that will finally make us feel complete.I especially like the musical instruments and the sound design. The song feels almost restless, as if the music itself is constantly searching for something that it cannot quite find.5. EgyptThis one feels mysterious and theatrical. It has a strong progressive-rock feeling to me, although it also sounds experimental and almost cinematic. The music creates the impression of travelling through a strange landscape. I like how different this song feels from the more intimate pieces on the album.6. The Wedding ListSuch a great song. I love the dramatic progression and the way the story unfolds. Kate Bush almost seems to be telling a fairy tale before sleep, but it is a very dark fairy tale. The music gradually becomes more intense, and the story feels increasingly dramatic. I really enjoy how she combines storytelling, theatrical performance, and music.7. ViolinSuper rock'n'roll and incredibly energetic. This song feels wild and almost uncontrollable. It has a completely different energy from the quieter and more mysterious songs on the album. I especially like the feeling of movement and excitement it creates.8. The Infant KissSuper creepy.The song is deeply unsettling. What makes it even more disturbing is the contrast between the beautiful, almost delicate sound and the uncomfortable subject matter. It creates a feeling that something is not quite right, even when the music itself sounds beautiful.9. Night Scented StockExtremely beautiful. This song creates such a delicate and almost dreamlike atmosphere. It feels as if the music is floating rather than moving forward. Once again, Kate Bush's voice contributes enormously to this feeling. It elevates my soul and creates a sense of peace and mystery.10. Army DreamersI love this song. It is heartbreaking and sad, but there is also something very beautiful and restrained about it. The sound feels almost permeated by sadness.The song is about a mother grieving for her son who has died as a soldier. But listening to it today, I could not help thinking about my own generation. Many young people were raised with the idea that the world was moving toward peace, cooperation, and friendship between countries. Hearing a song about a young life being destroyed by war therefore feels painfully relevant today.What makes the song especially powerful is that it does not sound aggressive. It sounds almost gentle, which makes the tragedy even stronger.11. BreathingThis is probably the song that shocked me the most.The song is written from the perspective of a fetus that is still inside the womb but is already aware of the terrifying world outside. The fetus is frightened by nuclear destruction and wonders what kind of world it is going to be born into.The line about dying "without" breathing is especially powerful because the word remains incomplete until the very end. Only then do we understand what is missing: breathing itself. The song connects the most basic condition of life with the possibility of nuclear destruction.And this is what makes the song so frighteningly relevant. It was written decades ago, but the fear behind it has not disappeared. It is deeply disturbing that humanity is still capable of threatening itself with weapons that could destroy the world. The song makes me think about how reckless it is to treat such a possibility as a political instrument.So, Never for Ever feels to me like an album about things that are difficult to explain directly: love, fear, family, death, war, desire, memory, and the strange feeling of being alive. What I admire most is her ability to transform emotions into characters, voices, and almost theatrical scenes, so the listener can experience the world she is creating.

items.body: Review by anomalocaris — This is an album I really love.Cressida's second album 'Asylum' differs quite a lot from their debut album. I will admit that I haven't listened to the entirety of their first album, but from the few songs I've heard, it sounds like some pretty decent rock. Asylum brings a new symphonic sound with some neat orchestrations. This is an album where every song (to me) feels basically perfect. You have 'Munich' and 'Let Them Come When They Will' which are your longer prog compositions, then there's 'Asylum', 'Goodbye Post Office Tower Goodbye', and 'Survivor' which are some shorter fun rock songs. 'Reprieved' is a short, jazzy, piano-led instrumental, and 'Lisa' is a great, shorter prog song with a lot of organs. I will say the song 'Summer Weekend Of A Lifetime' is quite boring to me and sort of feels like a filler song where the band had space for one more track and just threw together a little song. I love the orchestration in this album, particularly in the two longer, prog-ier tracks. 'Munich' also has this amazing epic sounding ending with a lot of brass instruments that I personally love. Those brass instruments can also be heard on the track 'Survivor'. This album is filled to the brim with organ and guitar solos, which I enjoy but may throw some listeners off.In short, if you're a fan of symphonic orchestrations and lots of guitar and organ solos, this is the perfect album for you.Oh yeah, did you know Mikael Akerfeldt of Opeth loves this band and album? (Stated in an interview with Progrock magazine in 2004)

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Sweden has a rich history of instrumental progressive rock bands, and the current generation ofartists has some really refreshing things to offer. Stockholm's very own G�sta Berling Saga is oneof these contemporary acts - initially an underground project that slowly gained recognition, thisfour-piece band is now a familiar name in prog circles, and as of 2026 have an impressive sevenstudio albums to their name. 2018 saw the release of 'ET EX' on Sony-owned label Inside Out Music,which would be the band's fifth album. GBS play a fascinating style of instrumental progressive rockthat incorporates elements of symphonic rock, RIO, space rock, and electronica, while the quality ofthe music they create ranges from experimental to dark and expressive - overall, the mixture ofinfluences this band exhibits is quite eclectic. However, 'ET EX' deviates a little from their firstcouple of albums, as it showcases a gloomy synth-laden electronic sound, which has been noted byother reviewers as well.It is almost as if there is a retro synthwave allusion going on, as the listener encounters a vastrange of synthesizer sounds, Mellotrons, and domineering electronic hooks. These are fused reallywell with the rock instruments, by the way, as we hear tons of angular guitar riffs and hypnotic,almost Krautrock-ish rhythms. The atmosphere of this album is undoubtedly darker, but the music isso inventive and tense that one might not necessarily notice the contrasting moods. And so, thesolemn opener 'Veras Tema' leads us to the nearly 8-minute-long song 'The Shortcomings ofEfficiency', where some serpentine guitars forge an upbeat, epic-sounding prog that is quitemesmerizing, too. This is the only track containing vocals, incidentally, as sang by guest musicianMichael Berdan. 'Square 5' is another lengthy composition introducing some wandering electronicsounds, as the music spirals beautifully around the listener, while 'Over and Out' carries a darksynthwave retro feel, which is delightful in a way. 'Capercaillie...' is another peculiar trackreplete with hefty electronics, while the closing track 'Fundament', supposedly the album'scenterpiece, offers a variety of unusual ideas, blending quite naturally G�sta Berling Saga'sexperimental style with the overt 80s influence of 'ET EX'.There is a particularity to this album, meaning that it won't appeal to every single listener, butthe music is excellent all throughout and there is a lot to discover and dive into.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "The Blueprint Dives" is the fourth full-length studio album by Norwegian metal act Extol. The albumwas released through Century Media Records in February 2005. It�s the successor to "Synergy" fromAugust 2003. It would be the last release during their original run as Extol disbanding in 2007(they have since reunited). There have been a few lineup changes since "Synergy" as guitaristChrister Espevoll has been replaced by Ole Halvard Sveen and guitarist Ole B�rud has been replacedby a returning Tor Magne Glidje, who had a previous stint with Extol in the 1999-2001 periodalthough back then as the band�s bassist.Stylistically the material on "The Blueprint Dives" is in some ways a continuation of the technical/progressive metal style with Christian themed lyrics of "Synergy". The music features elements ofthrash metal and death metal just as "Synergy" did, but the harder edged metal elements havedecreased since the last album and there�s a lot more clean male singing on "The Blueprint Dives"than on the preceding album (harsh shouting vocals are still a part of the soundscape). Harmonyvocals are now also a part of the soundscape (already heard on album opener "Gloriana") and while"The Blueprint Dives" still features heavy riffs and drumming, it�s a very melodic and accessiblerelease, even touching alternative/heavy progressive rock territories once or twice. I guess this ishow it would sound if late era Death (the band) and late 1990s/early 2000s Enchant met up andcollaborated. Extol definitely have a unique sound which combines a lot of different musicalelements. The more concise songwriting approach of "Synergy" is continued on "The Blueprint Dives" which makesit a nicely accessible listening experience while still being sophisticated and challenging enoughnot to be easy listening. Extol are skilled composers and a very well playing unit too, soeverything on "The Blueprint Dives" is of a high quality. The same can be said about the soundproduction values. "The Blueprint Dives" features a powerful, clear, and detailed sound productionwhich suits the material perfectly. Upon conclusion "The Blueprint Dives" is an interesting stepforward for Extol. They may have lost a few fans because of the more melodic alternative rockapproach of some of the material (a track like "Lost In Dismay" probably won�t please that part ofthe fanbase), but praise must be given to them for the courage to keep evolving and they arguably dowhat they do with great passion and conviction. A 3.5 - 4 star (75%) rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — (In memory or Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett, 1945-2006, thank you for being my inspiration)Describing the two solo Syd Barrett records, is a difficult task, for a brief period of time between1965, to the early 1970's, Barrett shone bright like the sun in the sky, it is shocking to listen tohis latter works after listening through the whimsical fairy tale like psychedelia of "The piper atthe gates of dawn" and the first Pink Floyd singles, to the dark, gritty and minimalistic sound ofhis solo records (this particular style is way more accentuated on his last three Pink Floyd songs,only one of which was officially released on "A saucerful of secrets", the other 2 on the Earlyyears Pink Floyd box set). These two records illustrate a clear picture of what was going on in hislife during this difficult period for him, they act as autobiographical records if one is to analyzeart trying to get in the author's (this time, musicians) shoes, they're deeply personal and displayan amount of vulnerability seen in very few works, that's where the real impact of "The madcaplaughs" lies...it's the collapse and fall of a legend captured into music, forever to roam and findthose who need it in the right time.The overall aura the music has is somber, mellow, almost detached, yet fully captivating. Thecompositions are quite simple, usually a chord progression consisting on some major chordsintercalated with minor and minor 7 chords, with some chromatic elements and simple strumming on anacoustic guitar, this usually accompanied by Barrett's tired voice, that lazes softly over it alland an occasional synthesiser. The two exceptions that stand out to this rule here are the tracks"Octopus" (which, any musician will be captivated by, because of its strange progression andrhythmic structure) which has an upbeat tone with full band instrumentation and surreal, borderingdadaist lyrics (they remember me of Nicanor Parra in some ways! Although I doubt Barrett had everread Chilean poet Parra at this point I'm his life), and "No good trying", which is incrediblypsychedelic and feels like a mix between colourful yet dark spirals such as those seen in Van Gogh'spaintings and a dark, strong bitter tasting beverage, it also has full band instrumentation and thelyrics are the emotional pivot of the record, as these paint the clearest picture of what Barrettwas trying to express. Despite not being as psychedelic as his previous works, and it all being alittle more simple and amateurish, it's s collection of interesting songs, yes, they're not foreveryone and will not suit the taste of those who seek a complex, detail rich kind of music, butthose who love folk rock and want to get to know Barrett more, will love this kind of music!I really won't get too deep in the production, since it really isn't that special, it suits therecord very well and does a good job at keeping fidelity to the songs, nonetheless I'd like to addthat it was done by none other than his former bandmates and friends David Gilmour and RichardWrigth, who he wouldn't see for some years after the release of his two records, they also acted asstudio musicians (tis but a fun fact that adds even more emotional weight to the overallexperience).The picture the record paints is clear and speaks louder than any biography ever could, since it'scoming right out of our crazy diamond's soul, it serves to humanize the legend and to give acomforting (yet unsettling for those who know it's context) hug to the listener...if you're in foran emotional experience go on, but I warn you that it's not an easy listen and might not be foreveryone, but, if you like Pink Floyd, and want a refreshing record, you'll fall in love with this!Despite knowing he won't ever read this, since he's sadly passed in 2006, thank you very much,Roger, for being my inspiration and giving me moments of comfort amidst hardship, you'll be ineveryone's memories.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It was 1977...and it truly was a whirlwind with the number of scenes happening simultaneously. New York's CBGB club was a breeding ground where bands like Television, who were killing it with Marquee Moon, Blondie, and even the early B-52s, who were as wild as aliens from outer space who had arrived from the 1950s. It was against this backdrop that Talking Heads emerged; having started as a trio in 1975, and initially championed by Lou Reed, who, like John Cale, had seen them at CBGB, the group was ready to record once Jerry Harrison joined on rhythm guitar and keyboards.Between David Byrne's vocals, distinctive right from the start, and Chris Frantz's steel pan, the band had something unique... setting them apart from their peers on the scene, even though they sounded just as raw as everyone else in a live setting. But where they truly made a difference was in their songwriting; the songs had a peculiar construction, all springing from Byrne's mind. "New Feeling" was a prime example of this experimental approach, and the quartet sounded tight and well-oiled.Within the New Wave vehicle, they incorporated rock with punk-like energy, without actually being punk, as well as soul, country, and the backing vocals found in "Tentative Decisions"; meanwhile, traces of Velvet Underground influence can be glimpsed in "Happy Day." "No Compassion" is very interesting; Tina Weymouth's bass work really stands out. There was already a distinctive sound present in Brian Eno's solo work, specifically during his collaborations with Percy Jones, though not in a fusion style, and one can even draw a line connecting it to early R.E.M. in the early 80s."The Book I Read" showcases a powerful voice, one that still had some maturing to do but was already fully present, possessing something of the vocal richness of Adrian Belew. It features a closing coda that could easily fit onto a solo album by Belew, who would later go on to work with the band. A Latin vibe takes over "First Week / Last Week... Carefree," featuring a guest saxophonist (albeit an uncredited one)."Psycho Killer" will forever be the band's classic track, with its driving, funky, provocative opening and Byrne's "psychiatric" vocal delivery; he knew exactly what he was doing, much like Roger Daltrey stuttering his way through "My Generation." The music, phrasing, and lyrics all come together to create an immortal classic and one of many generational anthems. The guitar strumming echoes the cacophonies of The Velvet Underground, the band they grew up listening to."Pulled Up" brings the debut to a close with raw, high-octane energy, a first effort that still had details to refine, yet showcased a style destined to mature beautifully over the next three albums without sacrificing energy or originality. It defied conventions and labels, embracing the freedom found in appearing normal within a world that was (and remains) increasingly anything but.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Several changes had taken place since the debut of Dave Stewart's band; there was only one track featuring vocals by Peter Blegvad, and John Greaves was on bass. There is a greater presence of wind instruments, which slow down both the fast-paced guitar passages and the keyboard sections. At times, "The Bryden 2-Step (for Amphibians) Part 1" takes on a somewhat anthemic quality (like Freeway Jam, by Jeff Beck), while at other moments it becomes more playful and slightly distorted."The Collapso" continues in a rock vein, sharing common ground with U.K.; however, Dave Stewart's highly disruptive keyboard interventions form a strong trio with the bass and drums, joined by the guitar, creating an atonal atmosphere almost reminiscent of Gentle Giant, before revisiting the same melody with a shift in pitch and rhythm. 'The Collapso' becomes an essay of multiple variations on the same melody, yet always distinct.Squarer for Maud, featuring cello and oboe, occupies another dimension entirely; yet other Stewart-led bands also updated their sound in 1978, such as Egg, with far more complex pieces by Phil Miller that take on a dramatic quality thanks to the organ backing. The oboe plays free jazz, accompanied by the rest of the band at a frenetic pace, until the piano stands alone like an island amidst Peter Blegvad's spoken-word delivery, a moment of calm before Phil Miller's return. With a string section that could belong on an Art Zoyd album.Of Queues and Cures is definitely their most rock-oriented album, yet it is well-balanced with the Canterbury essence and a style featuring wild, distorted keyboards sharing the spotlight with the guitar on "Dreams Wide Awake", a track that feels like an endless jam session, yet contains a melody full of groove and emotion at its core. On "Binoculars," John Greaves sings, his effective deep voice tracing the sinuous melodies laid out by his bandmates, while Jimmy Hastings' flute offers a most welcome, sweet gift, adding sonic variety; the display case on the album cover, with its jars full of mysteries, recalls the school library that Malcolm McDowell and his friends stormed in Lindsay Anderson's 1968 film If.... Ten years later, Dave Stewart would storm listeners' ears, using trumpets and trombones to craft a melody that snapped us out of any trivial monotony."Phl'kat'n" is another nod, somewhere between Zeuhl and Zappa, that allows "The Bryden 2-Step (for Amphibians) Part 2" to kick off with an avant-garde flair, a cutting-edge spirit that sweeps everything before it; John Greaves on bass and Dave Stewart on keyboards launch into a solid jazz-rock section before plunging into the depths, as the title suggests, and quietly fading away... because one doesn't need to make noise to go down in history.

items.body: Jabulile Majola sings “Baba Wethu” as a dove worn down by its journey, “Ngijuba elifuna indawo yokuphumula“, crossing hills and gullies through steady rain in search of somewhere to rest. When the bird’s strength gives out it calls up to heaven, the same cry each time over a marching chant, “Ulaphi sekonakala“, “where are you when things fall apart”, to the Father the isiZulu title names. The bird calling out for a Father is a boy who was left. The lyric opens on “Uthando lwangishiya ngisase mncane”, love left him while he was still a child, and he sings it from his own life: his mother vanished when he was days old, and by the age of two a pastor’s family was raising him among 26 children in rural Greytown, KwaZulu-Natal. He took the name she left him. It is all he has of her. The prayer turns before it ends. Majola reaches for a hand, “esangithunga ndawonye”, the hand that stitched him together, and asks it to lead him through the mist and across to the far side, “Ithemba eliyongiwelisa ngaphesheya”, the hope that will carry him over. He opened the song too worn to go on and ends it asking to be carried the rest of the way. He wrote “Baba Wethu” with his oldest brother, Levit Phungula. The song opens IPASI, his coming debut album, and follows his 2025 EP Isitifiketi. The live take comes from the Baxter Theatre in Rondebosch, Cape Town, where Ross Dorkin of Cape Town afropop trio Beatenberg joins Majola on bass. Stream and listen to “Baba Wethu” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Jabulile Majola – Baba Wethu (Live at The Baxter Theatre) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: This is Deutsche Grammophon’s fourth album of Joe Hisaishi’s music. One recording (played by the Royal Philharmonic) is A Symphonic Celebration of selected film scores, but the others, including this latest release, focus on concert music. Metaphysica Amazon Presto Apple The album opens with Hisaishi’s Symphony No. 3 “Metaphysica”. The work was premiered by the New Japan Philharmonic in 2021 and was inspired by the music of Gustav Mahler: Hisaishi says it uses the same orchestration as Mahler’s first symphony, and it was programmed with that work at the premiere. The composer writes that the subtitle “Metaphysica” (Latin for “metaphysics”) refers to a philosophy “concerning the understanding of existence and knowledge.” The music “emphasizes logic that transcends sensation and experience,” and, in his words, “I aimed to create music composed solely of the movement of sound.” In three movements, the first (titled “existence”) is built around a rhythm “consisting of three sixteenth notes” that is heard in each movement, with “melodic movements that transform upon this foundation.” The second (“where are we going?”) grows from a single 26-measure phrase subjected to all manner of variations. The finale (“substance”) is built on a hexatonic scale which, in the composer’s words, is “placed on both the time and spatial axis.” I am hesitant to critique a composer’s style, as listeners’ tastes differ and my reaction may not be shared by others. So let me state straight away that Hisaishi is a minimalist, a school of composition I have struggled to understand and appreciate for most of my life. His orchestration is expert and was the most enjoyable aspect of my listening. One can find online descriptions of his memorable melodies, but I did not find that to be the case here. Nor does the symphony use expected Classical-Romantic structures: in the outer movements I listened for elements of sonata form, in which multiple themes are presented, developed, and recapitulated. Instead, Hisaishi builds his music by presenting a melodic motive and subjecting it to coloristic variation. That orchestration held my interest for a long stretch; Hisaishi’s music is atmospheric and cinematic. But the three-note rhythm meant to bind the three movements together was not evident to me, even after repeated listening, nor was the melodic writing memorable. The ostinatos and continuing variations felt overused, and by the third movement I struggled to stay focused on the music. Excepting continuous variation, I am not sure how Hisaishi’s music connects to Mahler’s symphonic world, though his notes on the symphony suggest that was his intent. Not a revelatory discovery for me, though others may react differently. Joe Hisaishi. Photo © Nick Rutter. The Harp Concerto was a joint commission by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Bordeaux National Opera, the Philharmonie de Paris, and the Singapore Symphony Orchestra, written for Emmanuel Ceysson, the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s principal harpist. Ceysson collaborated with the composer, both in Los Angeles and Japan, during its composition. Deutsche Grammophon’s notes state that the work “reimagines the expressive possibilities of the harp,” replacing “conventional notions of delicacy with driving rhythms, bold gestures, and striking emotional intensity.” The concerto proved a more engaging listening experience. I sensed less reliance on ostinato writing — or perhaps the more substantial melodic writing and Western harmonic progressions made it seem so. The writing is more memorable; even after the first listening, parts of the work remained in my head. And the music does succeed in reimagining the instrument’s expressive possibilities, especially in the outer movements, which feature dazzling playing from Ceysson. The highlight for me, though, was the poignant second movement, which ends with a substantial coda demonstrating both the technique and musicianship of the soloist. Disappointingly, the digital release does not include any liner notes. The Royal Philharmonic play splendidly, though they sound more engaged by the concerto than the symphony. The recording is spacious and clear. One assumes that with the composer conducting, the music goes exactly as he intends. If you enjoyed this album, also hear Joe Hisaishi in Vienna (Symphony No. 2, Viola Saga) | Joe Hisaishi Conducts (Hisaishi & Reich) | A Symphonic Celebration (Studio Ghibli) | de Maistre: Harp Concertos (Glière, Mosolov) The form can be filled in the actual website url.
